This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a stochastic control problem governed by a parabolic equation with the control variable affecting the diffusion coefficient, particularly with the presence of rough inputs causing diffusion drift. We first establish the smoothness of an optimal control when the state is smooth and provide a precise estimate of the $H^2$ norm of the state in terms of the $H^{1-\delta}$ norm of the control. We then develop a finite element method to approximate an optimal control and prove that it produces a convergent and stable numerical solution. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed scheme achieves an error rate of $($O$)(h + \sqrt{h}/\delta)$ when using piecewise linear elements in both two and three-dimensional domains. We also establish the convergence rate of $O$($h^{3/2} + \sqrt{h}/\delta$) when utilizing piecewise quadratic elements in two-dimensional domains. These error estimates are obtained through the duality argument and an improved estimate of the norm of the second derivative of the state. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method by applying it to a real-time PDE-constrained optimal control problem involving a heat equation with diffusion driven by stochastic processes and measurement noise. We use a mixed finite element method to solve the discrete problem and show the convergence of the scheme in the $L^2$ norm. We test the method using two different types of rough diffusion coefficients and compare the resulting solutions with their smooth counterparts. We also investigate the impact of the degree of the finite elements on the error when approximating the state and control using different types of elements. We observe that the proposed scheme produces a accurate solution for a wide range of time intervals and discrete steps, especially when using higher-order elements. We note that the use of high-order elements results in a significant improvement of the error when approximating the state and control when compared to lower-order elements, especially in three-dimensional domains. We believe that our research contributes to the development of efficient numerical methods that can solve stochastic control problems with rough inputs with a large range of time intervals and discrete steps. We also propose a preconditioning technique that can be used to accelerate the convergence of iterative solvers when solving large-scale systems of algebraic equations arising from the discretization of PDE-constrained optimal control problems. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. Ultimately, the level of detail in our anisotropy patterns at high energies should be exploitable through future, larger-scale detectors capable of pinpointing the exact locations of these energetic sources. This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a specific characteristic - nilpotency, building on a previous discovery that these algebras are solvable. The attempt to explore infinite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras reveals that they can be solvable but the nature of their nilpotency depends on the field in question. The analysis also covers power-associative Zinbiel algebras and provides examples of both finite and infinite-dimensional algebras to illustrate the concepts. The study ultimately leads to the classification of solvable Zinbiel algebras, with connections to the Grassmann envelope and the Lie conformal superalgebras. The work's results are further demonstrated through the examination of specific cases, including the Lie conformal superalgebras and the N-ary Schr\"oder Lie algebras. The study's findings are also applicable to the broader category of Poincar\'e-Birkhoff-Witt algebras. The paper's main conclusions are further highlighted in its final section. This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework enables identification of specific data quality characteristics, such as data completeness and accuracy, as well as more general properties like data consistency. Ultimately, our methodology provides a flexible strategy for handling inconsistencies, allowing it to be agnostic to specific application requirements and thus offering considerable flexibility. This research on handling inconsistencies can be applied to various data quality attributes, including those mentioned above, as well as others like data validity and validity dates. Additionally, our approach is applicable to diverse settings, including but not limited to, handling inconsistencies in tables containing missing values and functional relationships, valid date ranges, and valid values within specific sets. This work is also relevant to the handling of inconsistencies in tables without missing values, but with relationships between the table's attributes, like functional relationships, valid values within specific sets, and date ranges. This research was motivated by the challenges faced in handling data inconsistencies that arise during data integration processes, specifically when dealing with data quality attributes and relationships between the data's own attributes. This approach was tested on real-world examples of integrated data sets, demonstrating its practical utility in handling inconsistencies and deriving meaningful data quality measures, especially on a health-related data set and a student-related data set, where the approach revealed additional information on data entries, thus facilitating more precise and tailored cleaning processes. This approach also demonstrated its versatility on a previously defined artificial example, known as the T-Example, which showcases its capability to handle complex relationships and data quality attributes, even in scenarios with multiple inconsistencies and complex dependencies. This research provides a theoretical foundation for its approach, which was tested on multiple data sets, including a student data set, a health-related data set, the T-Example, and previously mentioned student and health-related data sets, which were used to validate the approach's applicability to diverse settings and its practical utility in deriving meaningful data quality measures that can be used to guide the cleaning process. This approach was compared with existing methods that handle inconsistencies, demonstrating its advantages over these methods, particularly in situations with missing values and complex relationships between the data itself, thus offering a more general solution that is more suitable for integrating large-scale data sets. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after observing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use a task model
based on Neural Descriptor Fields and ensure it is insensitive to the appearance of
different object instances by incorporating SE(3)-equivariance. This representation maintains the pose information between repeated attempts at the task, allowing for the repetition of tasks on new object instances from the same category. To train the task model, we create a synthetic environment where objects are manipulated in 3D space, using Real Virtual Worlds. We test the model on both simulated and real-world scenarios, using the Real Hand-Eye Dataset, and find it successfully replicates tasks on new instances of the same object class despite changes to orientation, scale, and configuration. Additionally, we demonstrate the efficacy of Neural Descriptor Fields in repeating tasks on different object instances from different categories, although this is more challenging. The code for Neural Descriptor Fields is available at https://github.com/robot-learning/ndf. The datasets used in this research are available at https://github.com/robot-learning/ndf-datasets. In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a basic optimization method on a non-convex function can eventually enter a region where the function becomes locally convex. To address this, we developed an inequality that enables us to analyze the properties of the optimization landscape surrounding the solutions produced by an approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm. Specifically, we applied our inequality to demonstrate the local convexity of a particular TAP free energy function, which is relevant to the Z2 synchronization problem and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. Additionally, our inequality led to a confirmation of a previous conjecture regarding the efficiency of a sampling algorithm in the "easy" regime of these models. Furthermore, our inequality facilitated the proof of a previous conjecture concerning the efficiency of the sampling algorithm in the "hard" regime, thereby establishing the asymptotic performance of the algorithm in this regime and obtaining further insights into the structure of the algorithm's solutions. Moreover, we derived an estimate of the minimum distance between the original variables and the solutions produced by the sampling algorithm in the "hard" regime. Lastly, our inequality led to a confirmation of a log-Sobolev inequality on the optimization landscape associated with the TAP free energy function in the "easy" regime, which is a significant improvement over an earlier result and has implications for the asymptotic performance of the sampling algorithm in this regime. While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been difficult. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team has been taking photometric measurements of the Pleiades star cluster for over two decades using the UK Infrared Telescope and has applied this technique to those observations. We calculated the calibration of our system as well as the vertical aerosol optical depth at several wavelengths by comparing the decline of the Pleiades' apparent magnitude with their intrinsic brightness and the scattering of light by the Earth's atmosphere is much more significant at shorter wavelengths. We used a global aerosol model to cross-reference and correlate our measurements with other data sources. Furthermore, we used the calibration and aerosol depth measurements to update the zero point of the Planck satellite's absolute calibration based on the Pleiades. We found that the calibration of the Planck satellite needs a 2.5 microJy adjustment per square unit of aerosol depth for frequencies below 353 GHz. We also found that the calibration of the Planck satellite varies seasonally, indicating a long-term instability of about 0.3 per cent over ten years, although we cannot pinpoint the cause of this variability. We used our data from 2005 to support the Erbenezer experiment's satellite calibration, which led to a adjustment of the Planck satellite's absolute calibration from 69.0 Jy to 68.375 Jy at 30 GHz. We also used our data from 2013 to support the re-calibration of the S Bands used in radio astronomy, which resulted in a calibration adjustment of 0.375 Jy per unit of aerosol depth for frequencies between 2 and 10 GHz. We believe our method can be applied to other photometric datasets of the Pleiades star cluster, which includes those from other telescopes, and we suggest future observations from a fixed, calibrated system with photometric standards like the Pleiades for atmospheric monitoring and satellite calibration. We also propose using future telescopes with wide-field capabilities and permanent targets like the Pleiades to observe the Earth's atmosphere with high-altitude photometry over a broad altitude range. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be divided into two primary categories based on how images are used: regression-based methods and ranking-based techniques. Regression-based models predict a 2D or 3D point on an object's surface, with the distance between this point and the estimated pose serving as the training loss. In contrast, ranking-based approaches train CNN to rank poses relative to each other, with the most accurate pose ranked first. Despite the effectiveness of these methods, both regression-based and ranking-based models are susceptible to overfitting, particularly when working with limited training data. To address this limitation, we propose an ensemble-based technique, Object Pose Mixture Model (OPMM), which models the object's pose distribution as a mixture of poses corresponding to different classes, trained using very few samples. We also introduce a novel ensemble loss function, Effective Loss (EffLoss), designed to enhance robustness by reducing the impact of noisy training data. OPMM is accompanied by a code release at https://github.com/zhanglei1997/Object_Pose_Mixture_Model. Experimental evaluations on the ModelNet40, SSEN, and SUN12D datasets demonstrate the ensemble-based technique's capability to handle low-data scenarios effectively and the effectiveness of EffLoss in preventing overfitting. On these datasets, we achieved the current state-of-the-art performance levels. When using larger datasets, our proposed method also shows its versatility in scaling with increased data. To further advance the field, we outline potential future research directions for the object pose estimation community. We have made the EffLoss function and OPMM code available at https://github.com/zhanglei1997/Object_Pose_Mixture_Model. To facilitate the comparison of future methods, we intend to update the EffLoss function regularly and refine the OPMM framework accordingly. To this end, we invite researchers to collaborate with us via the code repository. We look forward to seeing the impact of our work on the development of more effective object pose estimation models. We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address General Graphical Lasso
challenges. Based on the original work of Friedman (2007), Graphical Lasso
estimates a sparsely constructed inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from
multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$, initially introduced by Dempster (1972)
under Covariance Selection. The framework has been expanded to accommodate
hidden variables in Chandrasekaran (2012) and can jointly estimate multiple
inverse covariance matrices, as shown in Danaher (2013) and Tomasi (2018). The
GGLasso package supports both centralized and distributed computing architectures. It provides both convex and non-convex solutions to Graphical Lasso problems. Numerous numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations have been extensively tested and evaluated. Recent research focused on the performance of these methods in biomolecular simulations, particularly with regard to configurational averaging. Our study builds upon this previous work and provides a comprehensive analysis of commonly used methods, including Brownian dynamics, Brownian-Gaussian, and Gaussian dynamics. We examined the performance of these methods in-depth by assessing their ability to accurately determine configurational averages through rigorous mathematical analysis. Furthermore, our study evaluated the performance of these methods via numerical simulations of an explicit solvent model and a real-world protein simulation. The results obtained from these simulations validated our previous research findings and provided additional performance metrics for the methods in question. Ultimately, our study established the criteria for selecting suitable numerical methods in biomolecular simulations, revealing that all methods perform equally when determining potential energies but differ when considering other properties, such as kinetic energies and configurational averages. Consequently, we recommend adopting optimized versions of Brownian and Brownian-Gaussian dynamics in biomolecular simulations. Additionally, we developed OptimizerMD, an open-source software tool that enables users to select the most effective numerical methods for various simulation scenarios based on pre-computed performance metrics. Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using existing eigenvector centrality solutions, making it computationally efficient. Unlike other centrality measures, our approach ensures that our multi-layer eigenvector centrality values reflect the complexity of each layer and its respective impact on the network, providing a range of useful applications, including identifying influential nodes within each layer, determining the relative importance of each layer, and determining the overall centrality of each node in the combined network. Our approach is demonstrated through the analysis of real-world networks, including a case study highlighting the benefits of considering the geographic layer on node centrality values, as well as its computational efficiency compared to other methods. Our multi-layer eigenvector centrality framework offers various advantages over existing approaches and provides a range of practical applications for its use in real-world networks. Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra by combining the $R$-Lie algebra with the Poincar\'e Lie algebra using the Dirac representation. Now, we use these algebras to construct a quantum field theory in the $R$-Poincar\'e framework and apply them to scalar field theories in de Sitter spacetime. This surface seal regime, found within the 5-45 kilohertz frequency range following the initial impact, was examined using high-speed cameras and microphones to record both visually and audially the surrounding water. Researchers analyzed both visual and audio evidence to better understand the surface seal phenomenon and its development over time. By studying the formation of a crater and the subsequent wave patterns in the water, as well as the sounds produced during the process, valuable information was gathered about the movement and pressure exerted on the water by the sphere as it enters the surface. These findings, in the form of computer-generated images, can be utilized in water-entry research and have implications for reducing drag and minimizing the impact's secondary effects, such as the sphere's bounce off the water or the generation of air bubbles. Additionally, the recorded sounds can be employed in ultrasonic testing for detecting surface seal disruptions. Recently discovered dark excitons in semiconducting quantum dots have drawn a lot of interest due to their reduced non-radiative decay rates and diminished interaction with surroundings, making them more suitable than bright excitons for durable quantum memory. Nonetheless, research on dark excitons is hampered by the difficulty of directly detecting them, as they lack a significant optical transition and coupling with light. We propose an approach to create a coupled quantum dot - cavity system that can facilitate the direct optical injection of dark excitons through an out-of-resonance cavity, enabling their direct detection and allowing for the distinction of dark excitons from misidentified recombination of trapped holes. By using an idealized model, we demonstrate that a detuned cavity can significantly enhance the probability of dark exciton formation, thereby facilitating their direct detection. Additionally, we show that a coupled quantum dot - cavity system can exhibit both an increased lifetime and a distinctive signature in photodetector signals, making it feasible to identify dark excitons based on a unique optical signature. Ultimately, this approach could provide a means of exploring dark excitons through an optical channel, giving rise to new possibilities for investigating this emerging field. We anticipate that our findings will contribute to the development of an optical scheme for investigating dark excitons within quantum dot - cavity systems. A fundamental aspect of two-dimensional electronic lattices is their two-dimensional neonatal geometry, characterized by the occurrence of Dirac cones in their energy spectra.  This feature is common to graphene as well as other graphenic systems, including graphenic superlattices and knotted graphenic structures.  Due to the inflexibility of their geometry, Dirac cones are resistant to deformations caused by external magnetic fields.  In this study, we investigate graphenic square lattices subjected to varying magnetic fields and their resulting energy spectra with Dirac cones at their center.  Interestingly, these cones can shift in response to changes in the lattice's misfit parameter rather than the magnetic field strength.  Additionally, the appearance of folded Dirac cones is possible within the energy spectrum, especially when the lattice's misfit parameter is comparable to the distance between neighboring Bragg peaks in the Floquet spectrum.  Notably, a pseudo- Nicole-like spectrum can be obtained by adjusting the misfit parameter to half its original value.  This system also exhibits topological properties, as indicated by the presence of a Chern number of 2 in the energy spectrum around the Fermi level.  This means that a graphenic square lattice in a nicotinic phase can act as a topological source for a nicotinic river with a Chern number of 2.  This phenomenon occurs over a wide range of the misfit parameter as well as within various ranges of the on-site potential and the next-nearest neighbor hoppings.  This study also reveals that nicotinic rivers can terminate at nicotinic oceans or meadows with flat energy spectra with zero-density modes at the Dirac points.  This means that nicotinic systems can harbor zero-energy modes at the Dirac points within their energy spectra.  This phenomenon is robust and can be realized in various two-dimensional electronic lattices with Dirac cones.  This study provides the nicotinic system parameters for experimental realization of zero-energy modes in graphene-based systems.  This robust phenomenon can be found in nicotinic square lattices with a misfit parameter of 0.8 or above, which corresponds to nicotinic systems with a Chern number of 2.  This means that nicotinic rivers with a Chern number of 2 can be generated using a misfit parameter of 0.8 or above in various two-dimensional electronic lattices with Dirac cones. Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters, where a coherent state is transformed into a state containing a single photon when it interacts with another state that contains just one photon. The success of this process relies on the states in question being able to distinguish between photon numbers, a trait that is lacking in traditional coherent states. In a recent study, we created SPCCSs with both lossy and lossless conditions using a quantum beam splitter, demonstrating their applicability in various real-world scenarios. These states exhibit a wide range of quantum characteristics, including Fock state generation rates, photon number distributions, entanglement, and noise spectra, all of which were analyzed through numerical simulations. Additionally, we demonstrated the feasibility of preparing these states in superconducting cavity systems, offering a practical means of generating SPCCSs and catalyzing Fock states using coherent light. These results pave the way for utilizing SPCCSs in quantum information applications, such as developing a threshold detection scheme for linear optics quantum computation. In this paper, we summarize our findings, in addition to presenting new research on the catalyzed states generated using a quantum beam splitter, which include not only SPCCSs but also states containing two photons, known as double-photon catalyzed coherent states (DPCCSs). We have the capability to generate these states in both lossy and lossless conditions and have analyzed their corresponding quantum characteristics. Furthermore, we have also explored the possibility of creating these states in a system consisting of two coupled optical cavities, offering another practical means of generating these states, which can be realized using a variety of physical systems, including nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond. These states can be utilized in various quantum information applications, including catalyzing two-photon states from coherent light. In this paper, we also examine the effectiveness of using SPCCSs and DPCCSs in this particular application, in addition to comparing the quantum characteristics of these states in both lossy and lossless conditions. Finally, we discuss the practical means of generating these states in physical systems, in addition to proposing a scheme for detecting linear optics quantum computations using SPCCSs and DPCCSs in a threshold detection setting. This approach can significantly enhance the reliability of linear optics quantum computations by reducing the minimum number of photon measurements required from four to two. This, in turn, can lead to an increase in the computation duration

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism. Furthermore, we obtain the complex coefficients of the Riemann tensor, demonstrating its equivalence to the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the self-dual case. Ultimately, this review demonstrates the process of converting the complex self-dual Riemann tensor back to its original form within the standard Minkowski space basis. Additionally, we derive the complex coefficients of the Einstein tensor and its trace, as well as the trace of the Riemann tensor in the self-dual context. Consequently, we can now convert these complex coefficients back to the standard Minkowski space basis, yielding the original form of the Einstein tensor and its trace in the self-dual context. This review is primarily aimed at graduate students and researchers seeking an in-depth understanding of how bivectors are treated within the Newman-Penrose formalism, particularly in relation to solving Einstein's field equations for complex self-dual electromagnetic fields. This review is also relevant to researchers working on solving Einstein's field equations in the context of Kaluza-Klein theory and higher-dimensional General Relativity. This review is accompanied by an appendix that provides detailed information on converting the complex self-dual Riemann tensor from the Newman-Penrose basis to the standard Minkowski space basis, including a step-by-step explanation of the necessary calculations. This appendix also includes a review of the fundamental principles of the Newman-Penrose formalism, including the definition of the complex null tetrad basis and the calculation of the Riemann tensor in this basis. This appendix further includes a discussion on how the Weyl tensor is used to convert the complex coefficients of the Riemann tensor back to the standard Minkowski space basis. A recent framework combining artificial neural networks and mixed integer linear programming for designing chemical compounds has been built upon to create a new method for polymer inference. This new method incorporates a unique way of depicting polymers using monomers, new descriptors that capture their structure, and employs linear regression in the predictive framework. Computational trials have demonstrated that the proposed approach excels in predicting specific chemical properties in polymers, also successfully modeling compounds composed of up to 50 non-hydrogen atoms within a monomeric structure. Furthermore, compared to the initial framework, the proposed method has been shown to yield property-prediction results of equal quality in a significantly shorter computational time. An illustrative case study highlighting the capability of the proposed method to predict the solubility of polyfluoro compounds has been included. All the proposed models have been made available on the NEOS Server for Predictive Design, allowing users to design custom chemical compounds according to specific property targets. Additionally, the server provides access to a chemical compound database containing over 10,000 pre-designed polyfluoro compounds. This database can be searched by compound structure using the Tanimura similarity measure. Accurate detection of esophageal tumors from CT scans is challenging due to low contrast levels and the esophagus's complex curve, making automated methods a desirable alternative. Presently, deep learning-based techniques, especially 3D U-Net, have achieved high precision in tumor delineation but come with significant limitations when applied to resource-constrained environments due to substantial memory requirements and computation times. In search of a more efficient and practical solution, this study modifies 3D U-Net to create a novel architecture called ESNet, targeting esophageal tumor segmentation. ESNet significantly reduces memory usage by approximately ten times and computation time by approximately five times compared to 3D U-Net while maintaining high precision levels. This is achieved by significantly decreasing the number of parameters and spatial dimensions used, allowing for a wide range of applications, including real-time processing and embedded systems. Experimental results demonstrate that ESNet surpasses baseline models, achieving comparable performance with minimal sacrifices, and can be used for various tasks, including tumor segmentation, distance measurement, and CT image reconstruction. In practice, ESNet exhibits a 4 times faster processing speed and a 10 times smaller model size compared to 3D U-Net. In addition to its efficiency, ESNet also displays outstanding performance in distance measurement and CT image reconstruction tasks. In summary, this study proposes a highly efficient and versatile architecture called ESNet, with vast potential applications in the field of medical imaging. To facilitate progress, we recommend designing datasets that reflect real-life code-switching patterns and developing models that can handle both language interference and code-switching effectively. Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives. For instance, using human-object interaction tags or descriptions generated by current systems, which we have already shown are flawed. Further research is also possible, such as creating a learning system that can correct its own past mistakes or produce better descriptions when given previous attempts. Ultimately, a system that can improve existing descriptions without needing reference data as well as a measure to evaluate its ability to do so are necessary to advance image description technology. Note that system evaluation is not the only application of high-quality reference data. For instance, a large and well-curated dataset of descriptions is also valuable for many other tasks and could be used to train systems that describe images, not just generate general text. Such a system would require a deep understanding of visual concepts and is thus more difficult to deceive than current systems. For now, we have a system that is able to detect fake descriptions by analyzing their semantic connections to common visual experiences, without the need for extensive training or high-quality reference data. This knowledge is then applied to a relatively simple model that can efficiently generate descriptions for new images, without requiring massive amounts of training or relying on expensive models like large transformers. This discovery has significant implications for the future of image description technology, particularly in its potential to benefit visually impaired individuals more equitably, by prioritizing the needs of descriptor workers and ensuring system fairness and transparency. This is achieved by developing a system that describes specific visual experiences that are both common and important to describe, without relying on expensive models or vast amounts of training data. This is made possible by a novel approach that combines a simple, robust model with a unique way of collecting high-quality descriptor data, efficiently. This approach is also pioneering in its use of human-object interaction tags to gather accurate and diverse descriptor data. Such a system and method have practical applications in the future of image description technology, particularly in its ability to describe specific visual experiences with both simplicity and versatility. This is particularly evident in the design of a system that can effectively describe cooking recipes, without requiring massive amounts of training data or relying on expensive models, by prioritizing system fairness and the need for equal opportunities

Quantum field theory complexity is particularly hard to define, especially when moving beyond simple free models and their corresponding Gaussian representations. A promising approach to address this difficulty involves 1+1 dimensional conformal field theories, where the stress tensor decomposes into two components - a trace part that's easily defined, and a traceless part that's more challenging to understand. Recent studies have shown that the state and operator complexity can be effectively determined by analyzing the longest wavelength component of the stress tensor, specifically its average, variance, or root variance. Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. To address these challenges, we propose a theory-based approach that utilizes a formal semantics to evaluate the equivalence of understanding utterances. This approach has been demonstrated to enhance the precision of system behavior specifications, but also increases the difficulty of making these comparisons. To mitigate this drawback, we developed a utility that compares the meaning of utterances and provides our research framework, called ChatterTest, which is now available online. Although our research is primarily focused on developing a testing framework for conversational agents, the methods we have devised are applicable to related problems, such as evaluating dialogue system APIs and developing test suites for dialogue management systems. We have tested ChatterTest on a real-world application and our findings indicate that it can create comprehensive test suites with a relatively small amount of effort, and that the comparisons it makes are meaningful to developers although they may require some interpretation. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the growing issue of data fragmentation in the internet age. Unlike traditional methods that treat multiple datasets as individual entities, our proposed Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) model treats multiple fragmented datasets as a unified representation to enhance recommendation accuracy. Unlike traditional cross-domain recommendation models that require dense user or item interactions, our model leverages user or item sparse representations across multiple datasets to provide personalized recommendations. Furthermore, our model introduces a novel Domain Adaptation Module to bridge the gaps between fragmented datasets and a unified representation, thereby enhancing cross-domain recommendation performance. Our model also facilitates the incorporation of side information to enhance recommendation accuracy. Through extensive experiments on five real-world datasets, our model demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art cross-domain recommendation methods, achieving a notable 10.6% improvement in cross-domain recommendation performance. System resources and code are available at https://github.com/zhenghaozhou/MSDCR.

The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor. Furthermore, our findings show that even when faced with random disturbances, the agents will consistently choose the same meeting location, a phenomenon known as stickiness, and one that can be influenced by altering the parameters of their decision-making processes. Deep learning-based neural networks are compared to the Motivation Dynamics model in a subsequent experiment, revealing that the latter produces more accurate results in predicting the preferred meeting location. Lastly, we outline the scope for future research in relation to extending the Motivation Dynamics framework to accommodate multiple meeting places and autonomous entities with distinct social interactions. Human stickiness patterns are also discussed as a potential area of application. Systematic methods for validating complex models of autonomous systems through comparison with real-world data are generally underdeveloped, and this paper contributes an initial framework for achieving this goal. Systems with complex dynamics exhibiting stickiness behavior are challenging to model accurately and often require unconventional methodologies, such as applying bifurcation theory to decision-making models. This approach can be demonstrated through a simplified scenario of an autonomous mobile agent making repeated visits to specific locations, but similar models can also reflect intricate patterns of human behavior, such as adherence to traditional meeting places, which, in turn, can be influenced by changes in social and environmental conditions. In order to effectively evaluate and refine these complex models, it is necessary to develop a systematic framework for validating them using empirical data from real-world applications. In this context, a particular case study is presented involving a magpie population that gathers at specific tree feeding sites, and for which a previous Bifurcation-based Motivation Dynamics model has been developed to describe their behavior. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we successfully integrated T centers into a photonic platform by creating a waveguide filled with silicon containing these damage centers. By simulating and experimentally confirming the distribution of these defects within the device, we were able to determine the precise conditions required for uniform T center formation and minimize spin decoherence caused by nearby nuclear spins. As a result, we were able to achieve strong coupling between the photon and the electronic spin and demonstrate successful implementation of a photon-spin interface for quantum communication. Specifically, our device allowed for the creation of a 10-micron long interaction region with minimal spin loss and achieved a 10-dB photon-spin coupling strength ratio compared to decoherence channels. This breakthrough in T center-based silicon technology paves the way for efficient and reliable quantum communication devices within the O-band spectral region. In addition to quantum communication applications, this technology also provides a suitable platform for generating coherent light emitted from electronic and nuclear spins in silicon. Consequently, this could give rise to a novel method for creating a reliable quantum bit based on the zero-valley points in silicon. In the process, we developed a comprehensive silicon material model that incorporates phonon-assisted spontaneous light emission from electronic and nuclear spins, leading to a deeper understanding of the conditions required for reliable quantum bit creation. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the feasibility of using T centers in silicon to efficiently couple electronic and nuclear spins with a photonic system, paving the way for developing large-scale quantum devices with silicon quantum bits that incorporate a quantum interface based on the zero-valley points in silicon. Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. To achieve this, he developed a method of analyzing the intersection of conjugacy classes within a specific two-dimensional representation of the symplectic group, represented as a vector space over a field with an odd number of elements. Additionally, Springer demonstrated that class conjugacy can be determined using quadratic forms with a specific number of dimensions, ranging from two to 2n-1, within the same given field. These forms must have a non-degenerate discriminant and be isotropic when n is an even number not equal to two. Furthermore, he discovered a connection between these quadratic forms and the conjugacy classes within the orthogonal group O_{2n+1}(K), also known as the classical group. The translation of this thesis also includes an appendix where van der Kallen clarified certain unresolved issues related to Springer's research. In the process, he collaborated with Geerdenaad, Kato, Milham, O'Dwyer, and Tanty to resolve these unanswered questions. The translation further includes an update on the Sp_n conjugacy problem, which was later fully resolved by other mathematicians. The original thesis built upon the foundation established by Hans Samelson and was an early precursor to the work of Roger Carter on class conjugacy within the general linear group GL_n(K). The translation of this research also spans into the arena of Lie algebras, where Springer's findings on the symplectic algebra can be applied to determine the conjugacy classes of the symplectic algebra's automorphisms. The translation of this thesis marked a significant starting point for future research on the conjugacy classes within other classical groups, specifically the orthogonal and symplectic groups. The research it spawned resulted in several notable achievements, including the successful classification of the conjugacy classes within these groups of the same given field type. The translation of this thesis also played a crucial role in the development of related research on Lie algebras, Lie adjoint groups, and their corresponding conjugacy classes. A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing shortage of available kidney donors. Desensitization techniques are being developed to overcome these incompatibilities and expand access to life-saving transplants. We present DesensITize, an AI-assisted platform that aims to simplify the process of evaluating and refining the incompatibility matches for individual patients. By leveraging a collective understanding of the complex factors involved in incompatibility assessments and referrals, DesensITize fosters collaboration among healthcare professionals, patients, and medical specialists through a coordinated and data-driven approach. We have tested the platform with real-world data from the Health2Sync health information exchange network and Kidney National Network, and the results show that it can effectively identify suitable matches and efficiently manage referral processes for multiple patients and medical professionals. Furthermore, the platform's data-driven methodology enables it to pinpoint areas for improving matching processes and refining desensitization protocols. Ultimately, DesensITize has the potential to serve as a foundational framework for developing AI-powered solutions that address a wide range of desensitization challenges and related complications in kidney transplants. We have made the DesensITize platform publicly available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/kuikc/DesensITize. We invite healthcare professionals, researchers, and industry stakeholders to collaborate with us and contribute to the ongoing development of this platform. We have also launched the DesensITize Challenge 2024 to further refine the platform and encourage participants to submit their own desensitization protocols and compare them against established benchmarks. We have made the DesensITize Challenge 2024 dataset and guidelines available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/kuikc/DesensITize-Challenge-2024. We have also made the corresponding technical report available at the following link: https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.01633. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model by Nielson et al., exploring how it generates embeddings that mirror the distribution of terms within a specific text corpus. We initially establish that the model's NMF-based implementation can be interpreted through the prism of non-negative factorization. Subsequent analysis reveals that the derived factors capture distinct aspects of word co-occurrence patterns, which we term the "distribution of company" – a concept that can be applied beyond the word2vec model. By delving into mathematical derivations, we gain insights into the model's ability to replicate the original distribution of terms by combining the factors, along with associated theoretical and practical implications. Moreover, we outline the boundaries of the model's ability to represent diverse document collections and coarse taxonomies, including those with nuanced relationships between terms. Ultimately, this study's mathematical framework provides a rich foundation for future model extensions and improvements. This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDET systems as alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1].
Fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimisation problems are defined and formulated.
By leveraging an algorithm that utilizes fixed points, we derive the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput values for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems.
Numerical studies are conducted to evaluate and compare the performance of these two alternative systems with our previously proposed optimal solution.
The results indicate that the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems achieve comparable or even better performance than the optimal solution, especially when the number of base station antennas increases.
This performance advantage comes at the cost of reduced computational complexity.
The fair-throughput values of the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems scale linearly with the number of base station antennas, whereas the sum-throughput values remain unaffected.
This makes these two alternative systems particularly suitable for frequency bands that span multiple widebands, such as millimeter wave frequencies. The SISO-OFDM system has the added benefit of not requiring any additional hardware investments. The term IDET refers to Inter-Base Station Interference in wideband systems. The fair-throughput value is defined as the minimum throughputs that all base stations can achieve without any data transmission, while the sum-throughput value is the total data that can be transmitted to all base stations within the same wideband band. The article is concluded by proposing future research directions for IDET systems. The corresponding MATLAB code can be accessed from [2]. In multiagent learning settings with general information structures, Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) offer a relaxed notion of optimality compared to the ideal standard of Correlated Equilibria (CE). We address the challenge of achieving CoCE through learning-based methods, given that these methods typically aim for CE and may result in the players reaching a CE that is not optimal for some players. To overcome this issue, we develop a novel algorithm that enables a group of players to converge on a CCE that maximizes their collective payoff within their individual incentive constraints, without requiring prior knowledge of the underlying game parameters except for the number of players. We also prove that this algorithm is guaranteed to reach a state of CCE asymptotically, and under certain conditions, it will reach the CE that maximizes its payoff asymptotically. Furthermore, we show that this algorithm is universally optimal, even for games with an arbitrary number of players, and it does so without relying on any prior knowledge of the game parameters except for the number of players. We also compare our approach with existing learning-based methods that aim for CE and show that our approach provides a superior outcome for the players, equivalent to the value of the game, or the Shapley value, for a wide range of games. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in simulated environments, including a scenario with multiple players in a variety of games, including the prisoner's dilemma, the battle of the sexes, and the public goods game, and show that it outperforms the existing methods of XDL and DDL, which aim for CE, and yields significantly better outcomes for the players compared to these methods. We also compare our approach with the DDL approach in a large-scale game with 100 players and show that it produces more desirable outcomes for the players. We also validate our approach in a real-world scenario with Amazon Mechanical Turk workers, consisting of 15 players in a battle of the sexes game, and show that it yields more favorable outcomes for the players than the DDL approach. We also provide theoretical and experimental evidence that our approach meets the requirements for being a CCE while maximizing the collective payoff of the players, and that it compares favorably to existing methods in a wide range of games. Previously proven properties include the limiting mean of the final number of infected individuals as the infection rate approaches its threshold from above, the standard deviation growing indefinitely in comparison to the mean, and a precise formula for the standard deviation in proportion to the mean. Additionally, we examine the standard deviation of the time it takes for the epidemic to end, finding it increases exponentially as the infection rate nears its threshold from above, in contrast to a logarithmic relationship in a model without re-infection. Our analysis also includes a brief review of the model's assumptions and mathematical structure, including the use of the next-generation matrix and the SEIR model. These analyses were conducted using the Euler method for discrete time, and both the continuous and discrete time models produced comparable results. These findings were obtained by simulating a random epidemic on a population of 5 simulated subpopulations, with results verified to apply generally. Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. To streamline this process, we developed an automated framework called TUnkfIT, designed to seamlessly combine theoretical predictions by swiftly and accurately merging the results of various inputs of different processes. This suite of tools, tailored for use with popular probability density function fitting frameworks, notably ATKaFit, also includes customized tools for calibrating and validating PDF fits and a detailed guide to help users easily incorporate TUnkfIT into their workflow. By substantially simplifying the process of integrating theoretical predictions and probability density function fits, as well as probability density functions themselves, we hope to significantly expedite the progress of PDF fitting research. The underlying code for TUnkfIT is accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/ATKaFit/TUnkfIT. Users can access detailed documentation on the tools' usage there as well. To download the ATKaFit suite, including TUnkfIT, please visit https://github.com/ATKaFit/ATKaFit-The-ATKaFit-suite. To obtain ATKaFit, users should visit https://github.com/ATKaFit/ATKaFit. The current version of TUnkfIT is V1.0, released on 23 February 2024. The version of ATKaFit compatible with this version of TUnkfIT is V2.0, also released on 23 February 2024. The ATKaFit team hopes that TUnkfIT will greatly benefit the probability density function fitting community as a whole. To that end, we are more than happy to address any queries users might have regarding TUnkfIT, ATKaFit, or any related topic, at the email address the-atkafit@googlegroups.com. To report any issues with TUnkfIT, users should refer to the section on 'Reporting Issues' in the documentation available on GitHub. To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from multiple episodes and correct their own errors. However, the current approach means agents must use their own poor performance to improve future performance. This research introduces a new reinforcement learning framework that enables agents to prioritize the most informative past data and exclude poorly performed episodes that delay optimization. By dynamically selecting the most valuable experiences to retain and re-run, the agent can minimize costly mistakes and prioritize optimal behavior more efficiently. This novel approach is tested in various challenging scenarios, including a dynamic diffusion process, where it significantly outperforms traditional experience replay methods and alternative optimization strategies. This results in more stable and significantly improved policy optimization. Systematic analysis of the algorithm's performance is supported by theoretical validation of its key properties, including the stability of the policy estimates and the convergence of the optimization process. To apply this approach in real-time, the research develops a practical, efficient experience prioritization scheme, capable of balancing the diversity of experiences to prevent overfitting. This leads to a seamless, real-world application of the new framework, suitable for various domains, including robotics and autonomous driving. System implementation details are illustrated using a representative scenario - a simulated river flooding management problem. This domain is utilized to assess the experience prioritization scheme and validate the new framework in a realistic, large-scale domain. The corresponding code is available at https://github.com/yangzhongzhong/experience_prioritization. The current version of the code requires Python 3.8 or later, due to the introduction of structural pattern matching in Python 3.8, which is utilized to enhance experience diversity. The recommended reinforcement learning setup consists of a centralized critic with two separate simple neural networks, each containing 50 hidden units in one layer. The experience prioritization scheme is tested with 1000 experiences and a batch size of 256. The code utilizes the RiverFloodEnv V1.0, which is a centralized, multi-influencing-factor domain with dynamic diffusion processes, available at https://github.com/yangzhongzhong/river_flood_env. The experience prioritization scheme can be integrated into various existing reinforcement learning algorithms. The research develops a straightforward and efficient experience prioritization scheme based on the similarity between past and current experiences. This scheme ensures the diversity of experiences to prevent overfitting. The experience prioritization scheme is tested in a centralized, multi-influencing-factor domain with dynamic diffusion processes.

We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models. This program builds upon the existing GLAM code and incorporates an advanced multigrid method to efficiently handle simulations. MG-GLAM offers several advantages, including the ability to accurately simulate the effects of modified gravity on the distribution of galaxies and their surrounding environments, and it can be used to create highly detailed simulations of large-scale structures for a wide range of modified gravity scenarios. Furthermore, MG-GLAM is designed to be highly versatile and customizable, allowing users to easily integrate new modified gravity theories and variants, and it has been optimized for fast performance on high-performance computing platforms. By leveraging its speed and flexibility, MG-GLAM can be used to conduct an array of applications, from examining the imprint of modified gravity on the shapes of galaxy clusters to investigating the biases of galaxy surveys affected by altered gravitational forces. Ultimately, MG-GLAM can be used to create simulations that accurately capture the intricate patterns of the universe's evolution, thereby paving the way for more precise empirical tests of the fundamental laws of gravity within the universe. Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. We show that these can be viewed as being driven by multiple SLE evolving in time and provide a probabilistic interpretation of the associated radial Loewner equation. This work also explores the connection between multiple SLE and the Schramm-Loewner evolution in the disc, developing a framework that allows for the generation of a single SLE on the real line from a Loewner evolution in the disc driven by a single SLE in the upper half-plane. As a result, we obtain a pairing of the complex plane with a slit and associated Gaussian free fields, domains that evolve in time, and a Gaussian free field-valued process evolving in time, all of which are all conformally invariant. MediaWiki's 'WorkingWiki' is an open-source extension that converts a wiki
into a sophisticated collaborative platform for developing high-quality manuscripts
and software projects. Originally developed at McMaster University's Department
of Mathematics and Physics for student projects, WorkingWiki enables multiple users
to work together on a range of tasks by providing a range of features, including
real-time code validation, automated testing, and seamless integration with
popular programming languages like Python, R, and Julia, as well as shell commands
like Make and Makefiles. With WorkingWiki, you can create customizable checklists
to ensure your code adheres to specific guidelines and standards, manage and
organize your project's files using features like file dependencies and automatic
removal of unused files, and even develop sophisticated mathematical content using
LaTeX equations and various conversion tools, all while collaborating with others
in real-time using features like live chat, @mentions, and collaborative editing
of code snippets, mathematical expressions, and text. This document serves as a
comprehensive guide to WorkingWiki, including a detailed explanation of its
features, step-by-step installation instructions, and a tutorial on how to use
its code validation and testing capabilities. Moreover, it provides an in-depth
analysis of WorkingWiki's technical architecture, as well as instructions on how
to install it on local servers using Docker, along with examples of how to use
its API, customize its look using skins, and manage its permissions using
Role-Based Access Control. The full code for WorkingWiki is available on GitHub,
under the permissive Apache License 2.0. If you're interested in contributing
to WorkingWiki or want to try it out for yourself, please visit its website at
workingwiki.org. The underlying technology behind WorkingWiki can be adapted
to enhance the functionality of any MediaWiki installation, and its developers
welcome feedback and suggestions from the community. The development of
WorkingWiki was supported, in part, by the Natural Sciences and Engineering
Research Council of Canada (NSERC) and McMaster University's Faculty of Science
Knowledge Integration Initiative (FKII). The WorkingWiki team would like to
express its gratitude to the numerous individuals who contributed to its creation,
including, in particular, Andrew S. Endrick, Andrew J. Thaler, and the students
in the Department of Mathematics and Physics at McMaster University. The initial
idea for WorkingWiki was conceived as part of the course material for the
University of Toronto's 'CPH 841: Research Methods

To achieve this, the model is integrated into a previous study that used the same method to assess the linear flame noise emitted by a jet-powered flame through acoustic pressure fluctuations. Initially, the same approach as before is followed to analyze linear phenomena, but the study is then expanded to examine nonlinear aspects, including the growth of oscillations that can extinguish the flame and the development of the equation that describes this process. This limitation becomes particularly significant when examining nonlinear aspects of the equation, such as the formation of acoustic waves with increasing amplitude, which eventually lead to the flame's extinction. Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory.
Einstein's gravity equations are modified within this theory to yield a nonlocal
influence, which can be viewed as a average of the Einstein equations over a
brief time frame in the past. This average is calculated based on the current
and past states of the system. Nonlocal gravity theory only exerts an impact
on the irrotational component of gravitational fields. It has no influence on
the rotational part, which results in the nonlocal gravity theory being
reduced to the Brans-Dicke theory for scalar gravitational fields. The impact of
nonlocal effects on the rotational component of the gravitational field is
precluded due to its short-lived nature. As a result, nonlocal gravity only
manifests during the formation of black holes and during the final stages of
their merger with neutron stars. The characteristics of neutron stars in nonlocal gravity are compared with those obtained using the Brans-Dicke theory. The impact of nonlocal gravity on the properties of neutron stars is minimal at their birth but increases over time as a result of their irreversible decay. The maximum mass of neutron stars in nonlocal gravity remains unchanged but the minimum mass that leads to black hole formation is reduced from approximately two and a half solar masses to two and a quarter solar masses. The f-mode resonant frequency in nonlocal gravity is found to be zero, which implies that the gravitational wave emission caused by f-mode oscillations will not occur. The variation of the star's radius during the late stages of its life is also found to be zero in nonlocal gravity. The relationship between the star's mass and its binding energy in nonlocal gravity exhibits a universal pattern that is independent of the equation of state. The distribution of mass in nonlocal gravity shows a lognormal pattern with a mass cutoff at approximately two and a quarter solar masses. The time it takes for a neutron star to convert into a black hole following its formation is found to be very brief, in the order of milliseconds. The relationship between the star's radius and its mass in nonlocal gravity is found to be linear with a mass radius of approximately 12 kilometers. The range of mass radius in nonlocal gravity varies from approximately 15 to 20 kilometers. The range of the star's compactness in nonlocal gravity varies from approximately 7 to 9. Understanding how genomic elements influence specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of possible interactions. We've developed an efficient computational method to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, including SNPs associated with certain human traits, by showing they interact through protein-cytosol contacts or occur within the same protein-coding unit. Using this approach, we found that a significant portion of SNPs associated with traits occur at positions that interact with proteins binding to trait-related genes, implying these SNPs could modulate gene expression by altering binding sites. Specifically, for blood traits, protein-cytosol interactions explain a larger proportion of associated SNPs compared to immune cell-specific epigenetics, while for other traits, such as skin and liver traits, the explanatory power is similar in both cases. Additionally, we found that a substantial portion of SNPs associated with blood traits are located within genes whose expression levels correlate inversely with those of traits like anemia, suggesting these traits could be influenced by microevolutionary changes to specific SNPs. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that a significant number of associated SNPs occur within the same protein-coding units as trait-related genes, which can be explained by genomic duplications for some traits but not others. We also observed that associated SNPs within the same protein-coding units as trait-related genes tend to occur at positions that interact with proteins binding to other genes, which could imply a role for 'neighborhood effects' in the evolution of these traits. We have made our method's application to existing data open for further analysis on our dedicated website.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no radio emission suggest that some of these sources might be binary systems containing neutron stars. To better understand these relationships, a statistical analysis was performed on 19 of these sources that have repeated activity and demonstrated recurring patterns over the past decade. A notable pattern was observed where the time intervals between these repeat episodes decrease as the sources age, indicating that their orbital periods shorten due to mass transfer between the neutron star and its companion. This behavior is comparable to that seen in another type of variable sources, known as low mass X-ray binaries that have an isolated neutron star at their core and exhibit similar orbital period changes. However, unlike the latter group, no actual orbital periods were recorded for the sources within the Milky Way's center, yet based on their repeat activity patterns, it is estimated that their original periods likely ranged between one and a few days. Additionally, by using previous measurements of their luminosity, it is also possible to determine the masses of these neutron stars, resulting in a surprising discovery: their masses are significantly lower than previously thought, ranging from approximately 1.4 to 1.7 solar masses and indicating that they were formed as a result of a specific type of supernova explosion known as electron capture supernovae. If this finding is confirmed, it would provide valuable insights into the relationship between the formation and masses of these two types of supernovae. Moreover, since these sources are abundant within the Milky Way's center, it is also possible to use them as a means of determining the star formation history within this region, particularly the rate at which low mass stars are formed, as well as the mass distribution of neutron stars themselves. If a relationship between the repeat activity patterns and the surroundings' environment is established, it could also serve as a tool to study the dynamics of the Milky Way's center. Furthermore, if a connection between these sources and the surrounding environment is established, it may also be possible to use them as a means of studying the dynamics of the Milky Way's center, specifically the rate at which stars are consumed by the supermassive black hole at its core. Additionally, since these sources are likely binary systems containing neutron stars, their disappearance over time could be an indicator of the supermassive black hole's growth within the Milky Way's center. THz radiation enables the precise stimulation of vibrational frequencies in molecules and crystals, leading to the introduction of inertial influences on electrons. By drawing a comparison to classical mechanics, where circular motion generates Coriolis and centrifugal forces, analogous effects arise, specifically spin-rotation coupling, centrifugal field coupling, and the interplay of these forces with the spin-orbit and the redshift of energy levels. These effects can persist for a few picoseconds following the initial stimulation, and potentially amplifying their magnitude could make this approach a promising means of controlling localized quantum states and chemical reaction barriers via vibration. Moreover, this approach may also lead to the development of a quantum technology that relies on THz radiation in the picosecond range. The theoretical framework developed here can be applied to a range of systems, including diatomic molecules, fullerenes, and graphene, and has been tested against quantum simulations using second-order perturbation theory within Hartree-Fock. The resulting energy level differences as derived through the perturbation approach are comparable to those produced by ab initio simulations utilizing the ADIPS code. Improving neural conversational agents' ability to produce diverse, engaging responses in casual conversations is a challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces a new metric called Response Diversity Assumption (RDA), which quantifies the gap between the models' inherent diversity and human-generated conversation responses. We further propose a three-part framework to bridge this gap by fine-tuning the models using three related tasks: Natural Language Inference (NLI), Related Sentence Generation (RSG), and Contrastive Conversation Response Selection (CCRS). Our results show that despite achieving significant gains, current state-of-the-art models fall short of replicating human-level diversity, with a predicted diversity of only 24 compared to 10,000 for human-generated responses. By leveraging our RDA framework, we are able to increase the diversity of responses to 1,024. What's more, our research reveals that enhancing the models using NLI data leads to an increase in accurate inferences but does not necessarily boost diversity to unacceptable levels. Furthermore, our work highlights the challenges of evaluating response diversity manually and proposes a automatic, NLU-based method that reduces annotation costs by 90%. Our findings and methodology are relevant to the broader conversational AI community with a focus on evaluating and improving the diversity of conversational responses. The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars might be impacted by rotation due to the addition of centrifugal force and potential break-up caused by rapid spinning. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, leading to a broader acceptable mass range. This research was applied to model the development of sub-stellar objects. A critical mass window allowed for sustained energy generation, ending in a phase known as the Hayashi track. During this phase, stars experienced thermal relaxation oscillations as they spun up and cooled down. Ultimately, the mass range became too low for hydrogen burning, and the star exhausted its energy sources. This led to cooling as a low-luminosity white dwarf. The duration of this cooling period depended on mass, but always took place over millions of years. This study also explored the possibility of very low-mass stars experiencing hydrogen shell burning, a phase that could last up to 10 billion years before they cooled down to low-luminosity white dwarfs. This phase occurred when stars had initial masses between 0.015 and 0.017 solar masses. This research demonstrated how rotation and mass influenced the development of very low-mass stars, leading to possible outcomes such as sustained nuclear energy, cooling as low-luminosity white dwarfs, or experiencing hydrogen shell burning. This helped determine the minimum mass required for a sub-stellar object to experience hydrogen shell burning, rather than cooling as a white dwarf, which was found to be approximately 0.017 solar masses. This value was derived from computer simulations and remained unaffected by rotation rates. This study also highlighted the need for future computer simulations that model hydrogen shell burning in very low-mass stars, as well as cooling white dwarfs, in order to better understand the development of sub-stellar objects. This knowledge will be crucial for understanding future astronomical observations, particularly those related to microlensing events caused by these objects, which could reveal the distribution of very low-mass stars in our galaxy. This knowledge will also aid in the discovery of future astronomical phenomena, such as the detection of radio waves emitted by very low-mass stars that have entered a specific phase of cooling.
