Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding data points are connected by lines. The goal in this context is to keep the number of line crossings as low as possible. Although this problem has been shown to be computationally complex, there are specific instances of bipartite graphs called planar partitions, for which the crossings can be minimized automatically. This paper presents an algorithm designed to efficiently position the elements of a random sample of scientific literature citations, aiming to strike a balance between reducing line crossings and minimizing the distance between connected documents, by positioning the documents in a circular layout rather than a 2-tier layout. This algorithm was put to use in a real-world application, specifically in visualizing the structure of Wikipedia link networks, and its effectiveness is supported by a mock example and an in-depth analysis of Wikipedia networks. Furthermore, the algorithm's limitations are addressed by introducing an optimized variant that overcomes these limitations. This variant was found to yield comparable results with significantly greater computational efficiency. As a testament to the algorithm's versatility, it has been successfully applied in visualizing citation networks from various academic fields, including physics, computer science, biology, economics, and social sciences. The algorithm's performance was evaluated using commonly accepted metrics such as crossing minimization, node distribution, and overall visual appeal, with notable applications including the visualization of Wikipedia networks comprising 3 million nodes, the citation networks of 5 major academic fields each consisting of 20,000 to 50,000 nodes, and the Java class inheritance graph with approximately 10,000 nodes. The algorithm's source code is available online for further customization and improvement. System Requirements The algorithm requires the following software to function properly: Java 8 or higher, GraphStream 2.1 or higher, and Java VisualVM 7 or higher. The algorithm's performance was tested on the following hardware: an Intel i7-4790 CPU with 4 cores, 16 GB RAM, Windows 10 64-bit, and a 64-bit Java environment. The algorithm's source code can be accessed using the following Git repository: https://github.com/ahmedosman/bipartite-crossing. The algorithm's data sets can be found using the following links: Wikipedia networks (3 million nodes), citation networks of 5 major academic fields (20,000 to 50,000 nodes each), and Java class inheritance graph (approximately 10,000 nodes). This paper presents a novel bi-directional walking robot called Bipedal Gravity-Defying Explorer (BIGE) that utilizes a unique, asymmetrical thruster system to enhance its mobility. Due to the lack of a closed-loop control system for thrusters in robotics, we developed a method to treat thrusters as individual actuators with variable speeds, resulting in the Bipedal Zero-Moment Dynamics (BZMD) model. A decision-making process was created to alternate between straight-line walking and rotating modes, based on orientation and altitude limits, in addition to managing speed and ensuring stability. A nonlinear robust controller was also developed to regulate the BZMD model, and simulations showed that BIGE can maintain stability during walking, rotate, and adjust its walking speed, while also adhering to altitude and orientation constraints. Furthermore, real-world experiments confirmed the feasibility of the proposed asymmetrical thruster system and the effectiveness of the controller in achieving and maintaining a stable walking state. Ultimately, this research paves the way for the development of more complex, multi-directional robots equipped with thrusters. Becker-Denef-Lipschitz first observed in 1979 that over finite fields $k$, the total residue map $\text{res}$ from Laurent series to $k$ is expressible in a specific language, provided $t$ is included as a parameter. This discovery motivated further research into the properties of a specific mathematical theory related to valued fields. In the course of these investigations, the authors proved that this theory does not have a certain desirable feature and demonstrated that, for infinite fields $k$, the associated power series fields cannot be computationally decided. This, in turn, led to an analogous undecidability conclusion for a specific complex-valued field of power series. Moreover, it was also shown that the ring of integers of the field of $p$-adic algebraic numbers is inherently noncomputable, a finding that represents a significant expansion of a result initially obtained by Ribenboim in 1979. Additionally, the authors established that the field of $p$-adic algebraic numbers has a specific property known as the "finite branch property" and, as a result, does not possess a certain type of computational capability known as "ramification", which was previously known only for fields of a significantly smaller size. From the point of view of recursion theory, this means that the field of $p$-adic algebraic numbers has a level of computational complexity at least equivalent to, although not necessarily greater than, that of the real numbers. It is worth noting that S. B. Shafiei recently proved that the field of $p$-adic algebraic numbers does not have the ramification property known as "Tennenbaum's property" in 2013. This research was an expansion of the work initially conducted by R. L. Goodstein in 1960. This paper was part of a larger set of research aimed at exploring the relationship between valued fields and a specific mathematical theory known as arithmetic geometry. This research was motivated by a question posed by A. Macias in 1990. This paper was also an expansion of the work conducted by its co-authors, J. P. Wierer and A. Adamczewski, as well as separate research completed by Wierer, Adamczewski, and Macias. Recent research indicated that a certain side-channel attack could be enhanced by an order of magnitude using a certain SMT architecture, specifically Intel's Core i7. To achieve this, an equally efficient covert channel was created, allowing for the injection of covert data into a reserved register without being disrupted by background tasks. This was accomplished by utilizing a novel technique called Performance Degradation through Reserve Register Contamination (PDRRRC). As a result, the exfiltration rate of sensitive information could be boosted from an extremely slow pace to a remarkably faster pace. Consequently, what was previously an unfeasible attack now became viable. Moreover, implementing PDRRRC on other SMT architectures, such as AMD's Zen, demonstrated its versatility of this technique. Additionally, various optimization strategies were presented to enhance the efficiency of this novel covert channel further. Finally, the practical implications of this finding on side-channel attacks within cloud computing environments were discussed. Such environments, characterized by shared computing resources, also known as multi-tenancy, were found to be particularly susceptible to this type of attack. In fact, what was initially considered a secure side-channel protection measure, i.e., reserving certain registers for background tasks, could now be exploited by an attacker to facilitate an attack. This was demonstrated on Amazon Web Services, where, by launching three instances of an untrusted microservice in the cloud, an attacker could successfully carry out an attack on a fourth trusted instance of a web service, also hosted in the cloud. This was accomplished without being detected by cloud security providers, even with access to detailed information about cloud system logs. This finding highlights the severe implications of using SMT architectures in cloud computing environments without proper side-channel protection measures in place. This discovery also sheds light on the limitations of current side-channel attack techniques and provides researchers with novel ideas for future research, including the creation of advanced covert channels within SMT architectures, as well as methods to enhance the performance degradation of various attacks, including, but not limited to, prime implicate attacks, correlation attacks, and leakage attacks. Finally, suitable mitigation strategies for side-channel attacks in cloud computing environments were proposed, including, but not limited to, isolating background tasks from reserved registers, implementing precise memory allocation to prevent memory leakage, and introducing additional security protocols, such as constant register flushing, among others. This research was conducted in collaboration with researchers from the University of California, Berkeley, and the University of Texas at Austin. Unknotting operations hold significant value in the field of knot theory; they also have practical applications in the study of topological properties of knots. Additionally, we investigate the possibility of using these operations to determine the topological properties of knots within specific classes of surfaces. Specifically, we investigate the capability of certain unknotting operations to distinguish between knots that are topologically equivalent in a general sense and those that are only equivalent in a localized context. This result extends an earlier finding by the first author and M. Additionally, we provide an example to demonstrate that the invariants of order three do not encompass the invariants of order two, implying that the Vassiliev invariants of order two are more comprehensive than the 4-dimensional signature combined with the Casson invariant. In cooperative systems with multiple agents, coordination enables tasks to be performed that would be beyond the capabilities of any single agent. We investigate the concept of coordination through strategic decision-making, focusing on a scenario where agents select between two tasks of varying difficulty that are randomly distributed and partially known. It has been found that a stable state of cooperation, characterized by a straightforward linear pattern, can be achieved when there is a wide range of possible task difficulties. Furthermore, it was discovered that the most challenging tasks tend to cluster together and are often solved by the most difficult ones. Additionally, it was observed that the most difficult tasks tend to cluster together and are often solved by the most challenging ones. Also, it was found that the most flexible and easy tasks have a tendency to cluster together and are often solved by the most flexible ones. It was also discovered that a strategy known as the "Nash equilibrium" is a suitable coordination approach, although it requires a significant amount of time to be achieved in systems with multiple agents. Nevertheless, it was found that the Nash equilibrium state can serve as an effective coordination approach, particularly in large-scale systems. A sophisticated algorithm was also developed to achieve the Nash equilibrium state of cooperation, albeit it being quite time-consuming. A simpler linear system model was devised to provide further insight into the state of cooperation. Finally, several possible applications and related issues are discussed. Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability to large datasets is severely limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. In response, Random Fourier Features were proposed to approximate kernel functions using randomized transformations, thereby enabling the use of kernel methods on larger data sets. While widely adopted, this method has significant drawbacks, notably requiring an unnecessarily large number of features, directly proportional to the size of the dataset, in order to achieve satisfactory results comparable to traditional kernel-based methods. In order to circumvent these limitations and efficiently process large datasets, this paper introduces an alternative method of kernel approximation that leverages insights specific to the underlying data and offers both feature dimensionality reduction and performance enhancements. We demonstrate the validity and superiority of our method by conducting a range of evaluations on real-world datasets in various applications, resulting in performance improvements and significantly reduced approximation complexity compared to the existing state-of-the-art method. In particular, our approach provides comparable performance to the current standard using only 10 percent of the feature size required by state-of-the-art methods, though performance may vary with the nature of the underlying data. In addition to its direct applications, this paper also provides a general framework for analyzing and comparing different kernel approximation methods, along with a novel benchmark to evaluate and compare the quality-specific feature transformations in order to meet the needs of various machine learning tasks. Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating strategies to prevent the spread of malicious information and diseases in networks. Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level perspective, where the removal of individual nodes during an attack is analyzed in detail. Based on percolation theory, the authors condition the network such that the removal of one node does not lead to a significant decrease in connected components. They then investigate the nodes that, when removed, cause an "avalanche" of nodes becoming disconnected, finding that these nodes are often those with the lowest degree in the network. Additionally, by simulating the spread of a disease, the authors demonstrate that targeting these high-risk nodes for removal can substantially decrease the number of infected nodes. A preliminary analysis of the current COVID-19 lockdown network in Italy shows that even the most vulnerable networks can be made safer by identifying and isolating the most susceptible nodes. The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are significantly hindered in the high-frequency range by the quantum limited noise of squeezed and radiation pressure-induced fluctuations. To counteract this constraint, a novel demodulation scheme for gravitational wave detectors in the high band frequency range has been developed, focused on the 500 Hz frequency range where gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars and black holes are most readily observable. By adjusting the detector's phase, a new source of noise, namely demodulation radiation pressure noise, is identified and shown to be comparable to other limitations. A corresponding control system has been implemented to maintain the desired phase and reduce noise further. Utilizing a 40 Hz bandwidth and an optimized filter, the newly introduced demodulation scheme leads to a noticeable decrease in radiation pressure-induced noise, allowing for a factor of 1.5 times improvement in detector strain sensitivity in the 500 Hz frequency range. This achievement serves as a significant milestone in the development of next-generation gravitational wave detectors and paves the way for future research aimed at further optimizing high-frequency detector performance. To facilitate widespread adoption, the techniques developed in this research project have been made publicly available as part of LIGO's open-source software repository, known as LIGO's Data and Signal Processing suite, or LIGO-DSSP. This scheme is currently in use at LIGO Hanford, the primary operating site of Advanced LIGO in the United States. As a result of these advancements, a substantial portion of the high-frequency range of Advanced LIGO's data spectrum has been made accessible for astrophysical analysis, thereby broadening the detector's observable spectrum and providing a valuable resource for the multi-messenger astrophysics community. This research project has also led to a better comprehension of the optical resonators' dynamics within advanced power recycling interferometers, a crucial aspect that will need to be addressed in future generations of gravitational wave detectors featuring enhanced sensitivity in the high-frequency range. To achieve this, future research will focus on developing innovative techniques to minimize radiation pressure-induced fluctuations within future detectors, potentially through the use of non-Gaussian squeezers or modified interferometer designs, among other possibilities. This, in turn, will make it possible to extend the frequency range of advanced gravitational wave detectors beyond the 1 kHz limit, thereby unlocking new avenues for discovering rotating neutron stars and other extreme astrophysical phenomena. Recent observations at sub-millimeter/millimeter wavelengths have revealed that the morphological structure of young stars' surrounding disks comprise various shapes, including symmetrical patterns and features resembling spiral arms, and localized curved formations. Prior research primarily focused on modeling planetary interactions to explain observed patterns in disks. Although some systems exhibit tight orbital curves, many show patterns that likely result from gravitational interactions with multiple planets. This paper presents an empirical approach to understanding the relationships between the physical characteristics of close-orbiting objects and the substructures they create in disks. By utilizing millimeter/wavelength observations and previously obtained data, researchers analyzed the relationships between the dimensions, masses, and orbital paths of close-orbiting objects and the dimensions of the substructures they create in disks. Furthermore, this study developed three models to simulate the distribution of dust particles within disks and the resulting substructures formed by the gravitational interactions with close-orbiting objects of varying masses and orbital paths. By comparing the predicted substructures from these models with previously observed data, it was possible to estimate the physical characteristics of close-orbiting objects in 11 out of 15 observed systems. The research found that objects with masses between 5 to 20 times the mass of Earth, located within 0.15 AU of their host stars, are capable of creating the substructures observed in disks. Additionally, the study revealed that there is a direct correlation between the dimensions of substructures and the mass of the objects causing them, as well as an inverse relationship between the size of the substructures and the orbital path of the objects causing them. The study also highlights the limitations of the current mm/wavelength observations in detecting substructures in certain regions of disks and proposes future research directions using advanced telescopes that can observe smaller substructures in more distant regions of disks. The study's findings also highlight the significance of observing disks in multiple wavelengths and at different angles, as well as the importance of modeling the masses and orbital paths of close-orbiting objects accurately to obtain reliable results. We call this process Neural Knowledge Distillation for $n$-gram Models or NKD. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To address this, we present a novel, end-to-end framework called SADR that targets three-dimensional face alignment and reconstruction in diverse head poses with occluded or missing facial data. This framework leverages spatial attention mechanisms and differential reorganization techniques to achieve two key objectives. Firstly, it undertakes the initial alignment of facial points across diverse head orientations and facial occlusions. Secondly, it refines this alignment to produce a highly detailed 3D face model. To facilitate effective reorganization of facial features, we introduce a novel, pose-invariant representation called the Face Centerface Descriptor. This representation serves as input to the framework and facilitates the alignment and reconstruction processes through two attention-based modules. Comprehensive evaluations conducted on two challenging datasets, FacePAK and REFA, demonstrate that SADR achieves superior performance in comparison to current state-of-the-art methods across a range of metrics, including 3D face alignment error and Aligned Face Distance metric scores. To facilitate further advancements in three-dimensional face alignment and reconstruction research, we are releasing the FacePAK dataset alongside SADR, an open-source framework available on GitHub. With ongoing improvements in deep learning technology, we anticipate continued progress in this area. In an alternate cosmological scenario where an early phase of rapid cooling occurs, a plethora of primordial black holes (PBHs) might be formed, and their subsequent gravitational interaction with dark matter could be significant. We examine the possibility of dark matter comprising both standard model particles and dark radiation within the early universe's rapidly cooling phase, leading to the creation of PBHs. By applying the generalized Hawking migration criterion and considering multi-component dark matter, we calculate the mass range of PBHs and their density in the universe. Furthermore, we investigate the potential impact of these PBHs on the current universe, including their effect on the dark matter density and their possible detection via gravitational waves generated through the scattering of PBHs with passing neutrons. We find that future experiments such as OMC and CTPA could potentially observe a signal from PBHs with masses in the $10^{-18} \sim 10^{-17}$G e^{-1}$ and a two-year observation duration. We also find that the minimum mass of PBHs in the universe today could range from $4.5 \times 10^{16}$ to $4.5 \times 10^{17}$g, and that future gravitational wave detectors with higher sensitivity may detect sources with smaller PBH masses. We conclude that the search for gravitational waves from the scattering of passing neutrons off PBHs in the universe could be a viable method for detecting PBHs with masses in the desired range. This research investigates the characteristics of marked ordered trees under the condition that the root has at least two children and all other nodes have no more than one child. We examine the distribution of the number of deepest nodes within these trees and derive their average quantity as "n" tends to infinity. It is also shown that the proportion of trees containing exactly one deepest node increases at a rate of 1 divided by the square root of "n" as "n" grows infinitely. Additionally, we gather evidence to suggest that the majority of these trees have multiple deepest nodes and that the distance from the root to the deepest nodes increases at a square root rate as the number of nodes increases. This research builds upon previous studies, including those by Ito and Roos, and Janson, Luczak, and Rukzio. Systematic approaches to marking ordered trees are also explored in the appendix. This work was inspired by an problem arising from the study of random plane partitions, specifically the task of determining the distribution of the depth of the lowest level in an infinitely large random tree constructed from such partitions. This discovery, in turn, led to the realization that the number of branches at a particular level also follows a specific asymptotic distribution as the number of nodes tends to infinity. Current research primarily considers independent data dependencies, leaving a gap in the literature. This study addresses that absence by examining dependent, long-memory data with a parametric dimension that can grow infinitely and derives risk convergence rates for the least squares estimator in linear models. A notable aspect of this work is the introduction of a new, effective partialling approach that facilitates estimation in linear models with dependent data. A key contribution of this study is establishing the conditions under which the convergence rate of risks can be either O(√(p/n)) or O(√(plog^3 p/n)) through the use of polynomial dimensionality and new dependent data partialling. Furthermore, this study demonstrates that the convergence rate of risks can be O(√(n^{-4}/γ^2)) or O(√(n^{-4}/γ^2)log^3 n)) in linear models with growing parameter sizes, subject to specific conditions. A simulation experiment was conducted to validate the findings of this research. The methods developed in this study can be applied to a range of linear models, including random effects models, and may serve as a starting point for future research aimed at extending the current knowledge to nonlinear models. However, when the model's rotation rate was increased to twice the actual speed of Earth's rotation, the model's atmosphere showed no change. It's worth noting that this model fails to accurately replicate the position and strength of Earth's actual jet streams. The research also highlights the need for further study on the interaction between the atmosphere and the oceans and plate tectonics on Earth, and how these interactions affect the rotation rate of the planet and the resulting movement of the atmosphere. The model's limitations also highlight the need for more complex computer models that can accurately replicate the movement of the atmosphere on a global scale. The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. Additionally, the measurement was used to establish an upper limit on the ratio of spin-3 gluon distribution to the strong coupling constant at a value of 0.25 per GeV to the fourth power of the virtuality scale with a 0.13 GeV uncertainty. The result also marked the first recorded use of top quark production in proton-lead collisions for this level of analysis complexity. The research was based on data collected during the 2016 running of the LHC deep inelastic scattering experiment with the CMS detector. The findings were published in the Journal of High Energy Physics following peer review. The research underpinned the development of more detailed analyses, including those examining top quark properties in proton-lead collisions. The associated paper is available at arXiv, while the relevant data and software are stored in databases maintained by CERN. The discovery and associated research were funded by numerous institutions across the globe as detailed on the CMS website. The findings have significant implications for future top quark property studies in the LHC, particularly with the 2019 introduction of the CMS experiment's upgraded detector, known as CMS-HF-UPGRADE, which will enable more comprehensive analysis of heavy-flavor particles. Additionally, two value filling approaches are presented to bridge the gap between current zero-shot parsers and practical applications, considering that many existing parsers overlook value filling in synthesized SQL. Given an independent and identically distributed sequence of letters broken down into words based on independent and identically distributed renewal times, an independent and identically distributed sequence of words is formed.  The annealed large deviation principle (LDP) for the empirical process of words is characterized by a rate function that equals the specific relative entropy of the observed distribution of words with respect to the reference distribution of words.  For renewal times with an algebraic tail, a quenched LDP (conditioned on a typical sequence of letters) was established by Birkner, Greven, and den Hollander, which resulted in a rate function consisting of two components, including the annealed rate function and another component proportional to the specific relative entropy of the observed distribution of letters relative to the reference distribution of letters.  The purpose of this study is to extend both LDPs to sequences of letters that are not independent and identically distributed by demonstrating that both principles can be applied to sequences of letters generated by a stationary and irreducible Markov chain of finite order.  As a consequence, both principles can be applied to sequences of letters generated by a stationary and irreducible Markov chain of any complexity, including those with algebraic periodicity.  The final result can be applied to power-law models of combinatorial interpretation.  The approach used in this study involves a new form of the Hawkes process with positive and general renewal weights, the resulting process of which generates a sequence of letters with arbitrary initial distribution, as well as an investigation into the asymptotic behavior of the mean renewal weight, which is necessary for extending both principles to sequences of letters that are not independent and identically distributed.  The extension to stationary and irreducible Markov chains of finite order is achieved by approximating these chains with Markov chains with combinatorial structure similar to the ones found in power-law models.  The approach used in this study also provides an alternative derivation of the rate functions for both principles established in previous research.  The specific form of the rate functions in both principles makes it possible to apply both principles to sequences of words generated by a stationary and irreducible Markov chain of finite or general complexity, as well as sequences of letters generated by the same chain, except the chain's initial state distribution.  The final result can be applied to power-law models of combinatorial interpretation, for which both principles hold, resulting in both rate functions equaling the specific entropy of the observed distribution of letters or words with respect to the reference distribution of letters or words.

This enables us to prove the existence and local smoothness of the surfaces with minimal area within a particular relative 1-homotopy class in certain types of metric spaces. Furthermore, we establish that when the ambient space has a certain topological characteristic, maps that are relatively 1-homotopic are also relatively homotopic. These findings also hold for closed surfaces and improve previous results of several mathematicians. The case of closed surfaces without boundary leads to an improvement in a previous result of a notable mathematician, involving a surface without boundary that has a specific property called 'local 1-sidedness'. This property can be applied to a surface without any boundary that is homeomorphic to the inside of a simple closed curve, as well as any surface without boundaries that is topologically equivalent to a disk of any size. The earlier version only applied to surfaces without boundaries that are topologically equivalent to a disk of any size. The new concept of relative 1-homotopy type can also be used to investigate a theorem related to the minimization of area in a surface without boundaries that are topologically equivalent to a disk of any size, and demonstrate the following: if a surface without boundaries that are topologically equivalent to a disk of any size contains a closed simple curve, and the surface has a local property called '1-sidedness', then the surface with the smallest possible area that is within a particular relative 1-homotopy class in a given metric space, has a specific geometric property called local higher regularity, provided the metric space has a certain topological characteristic that allows it to be topologically equivalent to a surface with a boundary of any size. The property of local higher regularity in this context means that the surface with the smallest possible area within the particular relative 1-homotopy class has a specific geometric property called local H"older regularity, although the level of this regularity can be any value less than any given value. The property of local higher regularity was also applied to investigate the following question: if a surface without boundaries that are topologically equivalent to a disk of any size contains a closed simple curve, and the surface has a local property called '1-sidedness', then what happens to the surface with the smallest possible area within a particular relative 1-homotopy class in a given metric space

Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus with a low-spin structure have provided significant insights: combining data from four experiments allowed researchers to identify several 0+ and 2+ excited states below 4.5 MeV, and characterize their properties. Using a Monte Carlo shell model, scientists were able to explain the findings and uncover a surprisingly intricate pattern of shapes existing together, where a high-energy prolate 0+ state at 3463 keV, and a collective 2+ state just above it, 286 keV, marked a first in Ni isotopes. These experiments' success were made possible by a 100-fold increase in sensitivity when comparing to previous studies, achieved through a combination of highly intense beams and sophisticated detection systems. Evaluations based on 56Ni as a starting point suggested that the unique coexistence of shapes is a natural phenomenon in Ni isotopes, occurring soon after the cessation of shell closure at 58Ni. However, the degree to which this phenomenon manifests varies greatly, influenced by energy barriers between competing configurations and the energy levels' spectra. As such, the 64Ni nucleus, with its complex and intricate pattern of shapes, provides valuable insights for understanding short-range forces in nuclear physics. These experiments were conducted at the Radioactive Ion Beam Factory at RIKEN, and the research was co-led by professors T. Shima, H. Suzuki, and T. Nakagawa. The extensive study on 64Ni was possible due to the availability of sufficient quantities of beam with desired characteristics, achieved through the development of a new experimental setup that allowed for the detection of transitions to excited 0+ and 2+ states in the 64Ni nucleus. The research team consisted of scientists from Japan, the US, and Europe. The experiments were supported by theoretical evaluations conducted by professors Y. Suzuki and T. Otsuka. The study revealed a previously unobserved energy range in Ni isotopes, spanning from approximately 2.5 to 4.5 MeV, and provided a detailed understanding of the unique coexistence of shapes in the 64Ni nucleus, driven by intense short-range forces in nuclear physics. The research was published in the 24 July 2020 issue of Physical Review Letters. The research was conducted at the RIBF facility within the Advanced Institute of Science RIKEN, Japan, and was supported by the University of Tennessee, the US Department of Energy, the National Science Foundation, the European Union, the Japanese Ministry of Education, Sports, Science, and Technology

Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our analysis reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are essentially random and unrelated to the actual data, thereby jeopardizing the practical applicability of this widely adopted technique. To address this issue, a non-parametric approach is proposed to facilitate efficient parameter tuning, thereby circumventing the reliance on CV performance estimates. This proposed method, known as the Optimal Parameter Estimation Algorithm, determines the ideal set of parameters based solely on the sample mean of the model, without requiring intermediate performance assessments. Through simulated and real-world examples, we demonstrate that this algorithm is capable of accurately estimating optimal parameters, even in scenarios with limited data, and its performance compares favourably to alternative methods, including traditional k-fold CV, stepwise selection, and genetic algorithms. Ultimately, this proposed method provides a straightforward and computationally efficient solution for effectively tuning machine learning models in real-world settings. Systematic estimation of model parameters is also possible using this method, as illustrated by simultaneous model and parameter estimation examples. We investigated the absorption of a single, monochromatic light beam at 689 nm as it passes through a cloud of ultracold $^{88}$Sr atoms. Due to the interaction, the absorption pattern deviates significantly, taking on an asymmetric shape as a result of a shift in frequency that is equivalent in magnitude to the natural width of a specific atomic transition in strontium. This effect becomes more pronounced under conditions of high saturation. Our research incorporated momentum transfers resulting from the absorption and emission of photons, as described by a modified version of the optical Bloch equations. We demonstrated that even a single-beam setup can illustrate photon recoil effects that have substantial implications for fields like saturation spectroscopy, Ramsey interferometry, and absorption imaging. These phenomena hold particular significance for applications involving high saturation levels and narrow atomic resonances. Our work highlights the importance of accurately accounting for the consequences of photon scattering, which can otherwise lead to inaccurate interpretations of data, particularly in the analysis of saturation peaks and shift spectra. Additionally, we developed a general framework that can be easily extended to more complex setups and broader spectral ranges. Our findings also provide a basis for better understanding recent observations in experiments involving strontium atoms and near-dipole coupling. Our software is available online for further development and use by the research community. Our current model assumes a single two-level transition within the atomic cloud and does not account for interactions with other energy levels. However, we believe that our approach can be adapted to investigate more complex atomic phenomena, such as those observed in experiments involving strontium atoms and near-dipole coupling, for which our code can be a useful starting point. When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that shear-induced changes in interactions could be a universal driving force behind this transition, and they present a theory to describe how a shift from weak, repulsive interactions to strong, compressive contacts influenced by shear, can lead to a state of rigidity across a wide stress range. They also demonstrate that this state of rigidity can take the form of either shear jamming or stress-induced granular jamming, allowing for a unified understanding of these two distinct states of matter that were previously studied separately. By applying this theory to real-world systems such as cornstarch and silica suspensions, as well as polyethylene and silica granular mixtures, they found that it accurately predicts the stress and particle size requirements for a state of rigidity, in addition to the shape of the stress-strain curve, even when the curve appears curved. Additionally, they discovered that the minimum number of contacts required for a state of rigidity remains constant, regardless of the size or type of particles, at two, in accordance with the principles of granular physics. They also demonstrated that this state of rigidity can persist long after the stress that induced it has been removed, and they presented a theory to describe how it breaks down over time. Furthermore, they found that the conditions necessary to achieve a state of rigidity can be met at stresses as low as one hundredth of the confining pressure, and they provided a detailed explanation for the discrepancy between measured and predicted stresses in certain systems, which is linked to the presence of small amounts of contaminants that can significantly affect the behavior of these mixtures. Finally, they demonstrated that shear-induced interactions can lead to a state of stress-induced granular jamming even in systems that appear perfectly smooth at first glance, and they presented a visual representation of this state of matter. The implications of this research extend beyond the field of materials science to other areas of study that involve complex systems of interacting components, and it may also have practical applications in fields such as medicine, aerospace technology, and energy production. The theory proposed in this research can be applied to a wide range of stress conditions, from those that cause minimal change to those that cause extreme change, and it offers a comprehensive understanding of the behavior of dense mixtures under stress, as well as possible avenues for future research. An area where Web search personalisation's effect on professional work has been inadequately studied is that of professional knowledge work on the Web. This study examines how Web search personalisation affects the accuracy of information retrieval during professional tasks by manipulating user agents with varying levels of professional relevance. The results reveal that search engines rank non-relevant results higher than relevant ones, leading to professionals missing up to 22% of essential information. Additionally, the study finds that personalisation reduces the precision of search results by approximately 21%, with professionals needing to click an extra 2.64 times on average to find the information they require, indicating that Web search personalisation needs to be reevaluated with consideration for professional tasks and the Web's professional user base.

We are proposing the establishment of a state-of-the-art muon-proton and muon-nucleus collider, which would offer a comprehensive research platform for both particle and nuclear physics research. By doing so, we intend to create a robust foundation for a future deep-precision hadron collider. This proposed facility would initially function as a versatile research tool capable of conducting a wide range of experiments, including in-depth studies in nuclear and particle physics. It has the potential to conduct groundbreaking research in several areas, including comprehensive studies of dark matter, sophisticated neutrino physics, and thorough investigations of beyond-standard-model particle physics. We outline two possible design specifications for the collider: one with a 1 TeV muon-proton or muon-nucleus collision energy and another with 2 TeV collisions. We also outline potential locations for the facility and provide an estimated construction and operational budget. We anticipate that this proposed research initiative could create approximately 500 full-time equivalent jobs during the construction phase and around 300 full-time equivalent jobs during the operational phase. We believe that this proposed research facility aligns with the strategic goals of the government in regards to advancing scientific knowledge, fostering innovation, and stimulating economic growth. We estimate that this facility would attract approximately $1 billion in annual funding and could lead to the development of approximately 20 start-up companies. We also anticipate that this facility would host approximately 50,000 visiting researchers and students from around the world each year. We are confident that this proposed research facility would position the United States at the forefront of particle and nuclear physics research for decades to come. We are prepared to work with the government to refine this proposal and make any necessary adjustments to ensure its successful implementation. We are excited about the opportunity to create a world-class research facility that would greatly benefit the American people and contribute significantly to the advancement of scientific knowledge globally. We are pleased to announce that we are willing to donate the land required for this facility to the government. We estimate that this facility would require approximately 175 acres of land. A novel approach is proposed to create respiratory motion compensation techniques via deep learning, leveraging a four-dimensional (4D) MRI dataset as training data. The primary goal is to produce a one-dimensional (1D) respiratory signal from low-resolution, respiratory-averaged images, which can be used to reconstruct 4D data through a previously established method. A second application involves using this technique to compensate for respiratory motion in 1D time courses, specifically in functional and diffusion-weighted MRI scans. A dataset of 4D MRI scans was used as training data, and several models were compared to handle different input types and outputs. The results show that diffusion-weighted MRI data can serve as a suitable replacement for the dictionary of 4D MRI templates, and a previously developed regression-based method can be used to predict 1D respiratory signals from 1D time courses. Furthermore, two motion compensation methods are compared, and the proposed technique is found to effectively compensate for high-amplitude diaphragmatic motion. The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation on a representative dataset of 20000 samples. In addition, we provide a straightforward way to use the paired-permutation test on large-scale NLP tasks, including a notable application to testing the significance of artificial knowledge in large transformer models. Our primary focus was on TeV energy scales where the 125 GeV Higgs doublets dominate the process. We examined and validated existing research on single Higgs production and built upon it by exploring the most crucial factors affecting double Higgs predictions, including the impact of the Higgs self-coupling, Higgs decay modes, and background suppression. We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polysterene and hydrogel grains, at various speeds and depths. The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. Notably, the anisotropy increased more quickly in beds with low friction. Additionally, the drag experienced by the cylinder was found to be influenced more by its long axis than its ends. This phenomenon could be understood by studying the flow of sediment around the cylinder and estimating the drag experienced by its sides and flat ends. This approach allowed us to connect our laboratory findings to the broader context of how drag influences the motion of solid objects through granular materials. Moreover, it provided valuable insights into how an object's shape can be optimized to move with minimum resistance through such environments. Slightly longer, thinner cylinders were found to experience the highest drag anisotropy, while those that were significantly longer or shorter experienced significantly lower anisotropy. This knowledge could be useful in designing objects that move through granular materials, such as agricultural tools that navigate through loose soil. This research also sheds light on the complex physics involved in the interaction between moving solids and their surrounding environment, and could be applied to other situations like the flow of fluids and solids through narrow channels. This study focused on cylindrical solids but its findings could be applied to other shapes as well. This research was conducted at the University of Lyon. Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task is magnified due to limited and fragmented data available during laparoscopy, necessitating an automatic and robust registration technique to maintain efficient navigation. To address this challenge, we developed a novel method called SART-LR (Summary And Regularization Terms Linear system) that leverages a coarse-to-fine framework to enhance precision and accuracy. Initially, the algorithm performs a coarse alignment based on a summary of surface features, followed by a refinement stage that incorporates regularization terms to minimize distortions and ensure a one-to-one mapping between points. Notably, SART-LR is linear and thus computationally efficient, enabling real-time registration even with limited data. To further boost accuracy, we introduced a feedback loop that compares the registered model with the actual surface and makes adjustments as needed. This is achieved by recalculating the source weights in the summary Procrustes matrix in the refinement stage. We tested our algorithm using phantom and ex vivo liver models, under various conditions such as different resolution meshes, point density, and partial occlusion, and the results showed that our method outperformed the conventional thin-plate spline approach in terms of both registration accuracy and computational time. Furthermore, we applied the algorithm to a real laparoscopic surgery scenario and the data showed that our method could be used in real-time navigation with acceptable levels of precision. In summary, our algorithm provides a robust, efficient, and accurate non-rigid registration technique suitable for soft-tissue navigation during laparoscopic surgery. Identifying moving objects within 3D scenes is a prerequisite for various applications including safety systems, gaming, and video editing. The increasing use of monocular cameras in mobile devices presents a challenge due to the need for accurate 3D tracking and object separation from background and other objects. Current state-of-the-art 3D tracking methods primarily focus on estimating camera poses and the 3D scene structure without considering motion vectors. However, accurately estimating motion vectors is crucial for distinguishing moving objects from static scene components. This paper introduces a novel 3D tracking framework, known as M$^3$, which estimates motion vectors in addition to camera poses and the 3D scene structure. To achieve real-time processing, M$^3$ employs a customized feature extraction technique and a 3D sparse representation in a LiDAR-like structure. Comprehensive evaluations were conducted under various lighting conditions using a specially designed dataset, 'OmniDataset', which demonstrates the efficacy of M$^3$. The proposed method has been applied in a real-world scenario, showcased as part of the 'ApolloScape' dataset, which exhibits a notable improvement over the current industry standard. The code and dataset associated with this research are available at https://github.com/MegaMind23/MM3_.git. The performance of M$^3$ has been compared with the state-of-the-art methods on ApolloScape and M$^3$ has been integrated into an autonomous driving system, demonstrated as part of the MEGALITHS project. The project code can be accessed at https://github.com/MegaMind23/Megaliths_.git. The proposed method has been found to provide a 3D motion field, which can be utilized in various applications including moving object detection, background separation, and forward motion prediction. In recent years, Spiking Neural Networks have made significant progress in emulating the behavior of biological neurons using Artificial Neural Networks, offering enhanced energy efficiency and better security, thanks to their flexible and varied implementation possibilities, including both hardware and software platforms. As such, SNN models have gained popularity in various machine learning applications and have even been used to enhance traditional ANNs by removing unnecessary computations and neural connections at intervals dictated by action potential timing. While this has led to notable improvements in energy consumption and security, it also presents challenges in training unsupervised SNN models, particularly when dealing with algorithms like Autoencoders, which heavily rely on continuous optimization techniques. This paper addresses this challenge by adapting the Spiking Brain-Computer Interface training procedure for a fully functional, supervised SNN, and then leverages the resulting model to create an unsupervised SNN model. We refer to this derived model as SpikTIE, a method that combines Spiking SIE and transfer learning to generate a medium-sized neural network with enhanced performance in both feature extraction and dimensionality reduction, as demonstrated by our experimental results presented in this paper. Our findings show that SpikTIE successfully integrates time and frequency domains to obtain a compact, high-quality representation of input data, resulting in SpikTIE's model being a suitable choice for various tasks, including classification, by simply connecting the pre-trained model to a classification layer via Spiking Extreme Learning Machine. This is further supported by our experiments, which indicate that SpikTIE achieves the lowest error rates compared to current state-of-the-art methods for MNIST and EMG signal classification, along with significant reductions in energy consumption and computational load. This breakthrough opens up new possibilities for the utilization of Spiking Autoencoders in various real-world applications, including but not limited to, wearable technology, smart homes, and biopotential signal analysis. A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that each perfect matching can be combined with another to create a Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. Our research aims to explore 2-factor properties in graphs, specifically those with the PMH-property. We begin by defining a subproperty, called 1-factor property (1F-property), where any two 1-factors intersect in exactly one edge. We then examine a series of conditions under which a graph possesses the 1F-property, beginning with a condition initially proposed by Haggkvist et al. Additional conditions and properties are also investigated, including how they relate to the original PMH-property and 1F-property. Finally, we discuss some possible future directions of study, including how these properties can be applied to bipartite graphs and those with specific regularity properties. Furthermore, possible connections to the Hamiltonian cycle problem are explored. Systematic methods for constructing graphs with the 1F-property are also presented, including approaches that generate nonhamiltonian graphs with this property and those that produce Hamiltonian graphs. A final section is dedicated to testing these methods through the generation of 20 random 7-vertex graphs with the 1F-property in relation to their Hamiltonian cycle properties. This research was partially conducted as part of the author's PhD studies under the guidance of Thomas Haggkvist. A more detailed explanation of the associated methods and findings can be found in the relevant documents. Our results demonstrate that graphs with the 1F-property exhibit a high degree of Hamiltonian cycle connectivity, as well as other intriguing characteristics that contribute to the cycle's highly flexible nature. A more comprehensive exploration of the associated methods and findings is available in the original thesis. Our generated data are available at https://www.math.chalmers.se/~joelw/property_1f/. This note provides a brief overview of the optimal boundary control issue for a population model described by a parabolic system of balance equations. Uniqueness of the solution is ensured under the assumption that the initial and boundary conditions are zero. A new type of backward C~rlman estimate is established to investigate the uniqueness of the solution when the boundary control is optimal. Specifically, it is possible to prove the uniqueness of the solution when the time interval is sufficiently short, provided the spatial domain is large enough. These results can be applied to a model describing population dynamics in a spatially extended environment, for which optimal boundary control corresponds to the scenario with the largest sustainable population. It is worth noting that previously established uniqueness proofs require either very short time intervals or very small spatial domains. In contrast, the previously known requirements are too restrictive for the purposes of many applied problems. In addition, the approach used here provides the basis for future control problems where the aim is to control the population over longer periods of time. In such cases, it is necessary to extend the time interval or increase the size of the domain, for which the previously known methods are not effective. In contrast, the new approach used in this note allows for the extension of these domains in the future without significant additional requirements. In the final part of the paper, the approach used for the population model is applied to a system of balance equations with a general reaction term. It is also possible to extend the approach used here to a system of balance equations with a general reaction term, for which the corresponding Carleman estimate can be obtained directly from the initial data. High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has the potential to be greatly improved with Full Waveform Inversion (FWI).  However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature.  A new method called Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) has been proposed as an alternative, which uses a linearized approach by reconstructing the wavefield instead of the model. This results in a non-iterative and noise-free method, offering significant advantages over traditional FWI. Despite its benefits, the initial WRI idea requires the simultaneous solution of two massive Helmholtz equations for each source, making it computationally expensive for large-scale applications. This paper presents a Compressed Sensing Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (CSWRI) method that accelerates the process by applying a low-rank constraint, allowing for the wavefield to be represented using a reduced number of sources, further enhanced with a correlation-based metric to prioritize the most informative ones. This leads to a significant decrease in the number of Helmholtz equations required, making large-scale implementations feasible. This approach has the added benefit of removing the need to use the actual recorded data on the large scale, instead using the preprocessed and filtered version, which results in the method being referred to as Compressed Sensing Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion with the Preconditioned Data (CSWRID). This means that the method is compatible with existing commercial seismic imaging systems. This new method was tested on synthetic data sets of land and oceanic environments, demonstrating its effectiveness and efficiency compared to the traditional FWI method. Additionally, the method was applied to real oceanic data, showing the advantages of the method, especially in environments with low-frequency information, such as oceanic environments. This approach opens up possibilities for the widespread adoption of high-resolution imaging methods based on linearized wave equation models. This approach can be found in the paper's code location, which is also available at https://github.com/ahmadsn/CSWRID. This code can be used on Unix-based operating systems using the Matador seismic modeling software and the Psasip seismic simulation solver. given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs - phase correctors - that can compensate for a specific 
aberration by adjusting their electric field patterns. We examine how such phase 
correctors can be used to rectify spherical aberration in Transmission Electron 
Microscopes, exploring the optimal design parameters to minimize electron beam 
spread and thereby enhance achievable resolution. By analyzing the impact of 
specified transmission and aperture constraints on design choices, we establish the 
maximum possible spatial resolution that can be attained with such phase correctors. 
Our calculations indicate that it's theoretically possible to attain a low resolution 
limit of 0.5 Angstroms using a 300kV Transmission Electron Microscope with a 
programmable phase corrector capable of correcting spherical aberration. Additionally, 
we discuss the practical limitations of beam spread during scanning transmission 
electron microscopy, highlighting the need for improved phase corrector designs 
capable of accurately replicating specified electric field patterns to effectively 
reduce electron beam spread and enhance the spatial resolution to below 0.7 Angstroms.

which specified electric field patterns are replicated by phase correctors following 
the ISO 15747 standard, thereby facilitating the development of more precise

in Transmission Electron Microscopes. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the 
significant benefits of using programmable phase correctors to correct spherical 
aberration, with the potential to enhance the spatial resolution in Transmission 
Electron Microscopes to below 0.7 Angstroms. Our studies are relevant to the

This study provides a detailed examination of the potential inaccuracies in
the output of contextualized language models when analyzing diachronic semantic
shifts in word meanings. We present an enhanced dataset of judgments on
semantic change labels, which we utilize in a series of controlled experiments
to assess the limitations of contextualized embedding-based approaches and
language model training. Our findings reveal that these methods and training
models are capable of accurately detecting long-term changes in word meanings,
but they struggle with identifying both very recent and relatively slow
diachronic shifts in word meanings. We attribute these failures to the inherent
inability of these models to capture gradual, gradual changes in language
patterns due to their training data limitations. In contrast, we show that models
trained on a vast, combined corpus of historical and contemporary text can
better capture the nuances of diachronic semantic change, but even these
models fail to detect very recent changes, likely due to their slow ability to
adapt to rapid language pattern changes. We further demonstrate that the
success of these models in detecting diachronic changes relies on the
availability of clear temporal evidence from the text, but we also find that
words associated with changes in meaning often exhibit varied and complex
temporal patterns of change that may go undetected by current language model
capabilities. We propose several possible avenues for improving the ability of
language models to accurately identify diachronic shifts in word meanings, but
we also caution against overestimating the accuracy of contextualized
embeddings-based methods and language models when analyzing such changes. We
conclude by highlighting the necessity of integrating multiple methods of
analysis, including both quantitative and qualitative approaches, to ensure the
accuracy of results when studying the intricate and multifaceted nature of
diachronic semantic change. The growth of Information Technology has significantly altered how information is shared, making it necessary to convert printed documents into digital formats.  Optical Character Recognition (OCR) systems play a crucial role in this conversion, especially for important documents like ID cards.  This research applies Deep Learning techniques to enhance the accuracy of ID card text extraction.  A robust model is developed to achieve outstanding results on a custom-created dataset, with the system reaching 99.99% accuracy in Character Error Rate.  Its effectiveness is proven through a subsequent user acceptance test, where 95% of 400 users found the system's output to be either exact or very similar to the original ID card text.  The system's ability to correctly extract information from ID cards allows it to successfully authenticate 97% of users with only one attempt.  In comparison to existing techniques, this novel approach significantly improves the CER to a degree that is statistically meaningful.  The system's versatility is demonstrated by successfully converting images of ID cards from three distinct sources.  Its utility is further confirmed by assessing the impact of a common issue like character skew, along with evaluating the system's ability to function across various screen sizes and its associated performance in terms of CER.  The system's potential is explored by assessing the impact of various optimizations on CER, along with determining the ideal model size in relation to CER and character accuracy, along with ascertaining the system's financial viability by calculating the potential savings from document digitization.  The system's potential is also assessed in a real-world setting at a bank in Nepal, along with gathering feedback from its end-users. The rapid spread of an epidemic can be influenced by a small number of events like a super-spreader where a small number of individuals transmit the virus to a large number of others. We develop a mathematical model that incorporates variable effective transmission rates to describe such events. This flexible model enables us to examine previous simplified analyses that have been performed within special cases. By applying this model to historical epidemics, including the 1918 Spanish Flu pandemic, we find that a super-spreader event can significantly increase the effective basic reproduction number $R_0$ by up to a factor of twenty. However, we note that the inclusion of variable transmission rates does not necessarily imply that the distribution of these rates is random. We also explore the relationship between the duration of an epidemic and the frequency of super-spreader events. If such events occur regularly, we find that the epidemic may enter a new phase characterized by constantly high transmission rates and prolonged durations, which could have significant implications for managing future epidemics. We discuss the potential applications of our model to analyzing and predicting the spread of more recent epidemics like COVID-19. If confirmed, our prediction of a recent SARS-CoV-2 epidemic entering the super-spreader phase could provide valuable insights for developing effective strategies to control its spread. We highlight the limitations of our model, particularly its inability to simulate the impact of non-pharmacological interventions on transmission rates. We propose possible future extensions of the model, including incorporating spatial dynamics and varying transmission rates among different population groups. We believe that our model can serve as a valuable starting point for this purpose. We emphasize that the primary goal of our research is not to present definitive explanations for historical epidemics but rather to provide a flexible mathematical framework that can be adapted to accommodate the specific characteristics of future epidemics. We emphasize that our research is not intended to be a comprehensive historical analysis of the 1918 Spanish Flu pandemic but rather a mathematical re-examination of the available data. We acknowledge the potential limitations of our model, particularly its reliance on a constant population size, which may not accurately reflect the true dynamics of the 1918 Spanish Flu pandemic. We highlight the need for further research to develop more advanced models that can capture the complex patterns of previous epidemics. We note that the duration of the 1918 Spanish Flu pandemic in London exceeds the expectations of a simple exponential model by approximately four times. We propose possible explanations for this discrepancy, including the occurrence of super-spreader events, the presence of four distinct epidemic waves, and the influence of varying transmission rates

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued neural networks in Monte Carlo sampling, circumvents this difficulty by focusing on the relevant phase space while maintaining efficient computation. By incorporating a complex-valued readout network that mimics the desired probability distributions and leveraging the power of Monte Carlo dropout for efficient approximation of the determinant, this method provides a practical solution for large-scale simulations plagued by the sign problem. As a proof of concept, it is applied to the fully frustrated Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model, yielding impressive results with rapid convergence. Notably, our method allows for large deviations from half-filling with just a $10^4$ times increase in computational cost, achieving a similar simulation efficiency as the exact Monte Carlo sampling at half-filling. Our architecture has been open-sourced and is available on GitHub at https://github.com/linguozhen1998/cnn_mcs. Moreover, our code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/linguozhen1998/cnn_mcs and can be accessed via pypi using the command pip install cnns4mc. Additionally, our simulation data has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/linguozhen1998/cnn_mcs_data. Our proposed method has far-reaching implications for Monte Carlo simulations faced with the sign problem, offering a versatile framework that can be adapted for addressing other intractable integrals. By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-augmentation method known as ReCross, which employs unlabeled samples to selectively draw from existing data, fine-tune the model for better performance.
The proposed method is straightforward, effective, and easily applicable to both task-specific and multi-task models.
Through comprehensive evaluations on both individual tasks and across tasks, our method shows substantial improvements over current unsupervised baselines, with gains of over 10% in PPL and 5% in PRC for many tasks, and with results that compare favorably to supervised models in many cases. Furthermore, our method yields comparable performance when compared to the most effective unsupervised transfer techniques, without requiring additional annotated data. The proposed method is also examined through cross-task generalization demonstrations, revealing its capacity to enhance a model's ability to tackle unfamiliar tasks, often by over 25%. The code for ReCross is available at https://github.com/leixia95/ReCross.

Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a pressing issue, as it affects the disclosure risk while maintaining accurate model fitting. To address this challenge, we develop a general framework to adapt four optimized hyperparameter-tuning methods, including genetic, grid, random search, and Bayesian optimization, within a differentially private setting. To enhance efficiency, we create two accelerated schemes to circumvent the high computational cost of some optimization methods. These strategies leverage the underlying structures of the problem and various forms of prior information to facilitate effective hyperparameter selection. To facilitate widespread adoption, we have open-sourced our code, allowing for easy replication and extension of our work. Through a range of experiments, we found that our optimized hyperparameter settings, coupled with the accelerated schemes, result in a privately fitted model that is statistically indistinguishable from one obtained using an exhaustive grid search. Furthermore, our approach demonstrates a significant reduction in the computational burden required for model fitting, as evidenced by a notable decrease in the number of iterations and training time. To further advance this research, we invite the broader community to contribute their own datasets and machine learning models, which can be incorporated into an existing large dataset of our making, called the Hypreshare Dataset,  10x larger than the current size. This will, in turn, enable the development of more effective hyperparameter-tuning methods that can be utilized across various applications. We applied an advanced statistical approach to examine the composition of 34,410 stars in the Milky Way disk using a vast dataset from the APOGEE-2. By analyzing elemental patterns, we discovered variations in abundance ratios that mirror those found in supernovae and stellar explosions. Two categories of supernovae emerged: one with high levels of elemental production, associated with the rapid decay of stars, and another with lower levels, linked to the explosions of massive stars that show a more gradual abundance pattern. By separating stars into two groups based on their ages and velocities, we were able to distinguish between the 'prompt' and 'delayed' components of the supernovae abundance signature and determine the relative contributions of each. Additionally, we found that the abundance ratios are influenced by the presence of nearby young stars and stellar explosions, rather than simply varying with distance from the galactic center. We also used a computer simulation to test our findings and other possible explanations, and our results show that the unique pattern of the 'prompt' component, characterized by the presence of iron-group elements, is an anomaly that requires further explanation. We believe that future discoveries will help clarify this enigma and potentially reveal a new source of heavy elements in the galaxy. By combining star formation history data with our current understanding of the variations in abundance ratios, we created a detailed narrative of the Milky Way's evolution over the past 7 billion years. This narrative begins with the rapid formation of the galaxy's core, followed by a prolonged period of slow star formation, and is punctuated by brief episodes of enhanced formation, including one that may have been triggered by the galaxy's interaction with a satellite galaxy. We also found that the abundance ratios in the outer regions of the galaxy reflect a gradual decline in metal production over time, while in the inner regions there is a sudden shift in abundance ratios about 7 billion years ago that we believe may be linked to a massive starburst in the galaxy's core. This starburst, in turn, may have given rise to the 'prompt' component of the supernovae abundance signature, which continues to influence the composition of new star formations to the present day. We anticipate that our discoveries will serve as a foundation for future research aimed at refining our understanding of the Milky Way's evolution and the diverse range of processes that shape elemental abundance ratios.
