Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been thoroughly explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, we develop a method to incorporate structured knowledge into LLMs through training on specific knowledge graph triples. Our approach allows for the utilization of both factual knowledge and relational information that LLMs can leverage for enhanced performance on various tasks. We demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained with our method surpass the performance of standard LLMs baselines in several areas, including relationship classification, sentence completion, and question-answering. Furthermore, we show that using structured knowledge rather than factual information from sentences enhances the effectiveness of our method, indicating that infusing structured knowledge provides a distinct advantage over using unstructured text knowledge. Our pre-trained models exhibit comparable performance to the current state-of-the-art models but are significantly simpler and more interpretable, given their reliance on fundamental knowledge that can be easily understood. We have made our models and training data available for public use.

Achieving a seamless visual experience and optimal system performance when displaying line joins on vector maps is crucial, as these maps are widely used in navigation applications. The issue arises because map data typically lacks sufficient detail at low zoom levels, where the display resolution is high and fine line joins may create display list overflows or lead to jerky animations. We present a technique called spatial anti-aliasing that mitigates the impact of line join aliasing at high resolutions and low zoom levels. This approach leverages a novel sampling pattern to capture the precise line join patterns and combines them with the alpha anti-aliasing technique to eliminate display list overflow and animation jitters. We also introduce a vector map rendering framework that includes a data-driven approach to determining optimal line styles based on map content and a set of predefined styles. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of spatial anti-aliasing and our rendering framework, which includes a visually appealing demo available at https://github.com/google/vector-map-anti-aliasing. This demo allows users to interact with a high-resolution, zoomable vector map that showcases the anti-aliasing technique and related issues with line joins, as well as examples of optimized line styles generated using the TIGER/Line2 format. Our rendering framework is part of the Android Maps API, which we plan to open-source in the future. We also propose several optimization strategies for reducing memory consumption and improving rendering efficiency, including a compressed display list and alpha anti-aliasing, which we believe are universally applicable to various vector map rendering platforms. Our evaluation shows that the use of compressed display lists can decrease memory usage by up to 50% and improve rendering performance by up to 30%. We further explore several line style optimization techniques, such as removing unnecessary geometries, compressing style data, and prioritizing geometries based on zoom levels, which we found can decrease memory consumption by up to 90% and improve rendering efficiency by up to 80%. We also examine various compression schemes for style data and compressed display lists and recommend the use of Huffman coding for style data and the use of a custom scheme for compressed display lists. We believe our research contributes significantly to the field of vector map rendering, particularly with regards to anti-aliasing techniques and optimized line style generation, which we plan to continue exploring in the future. We also hope that our evaluation of compression schemes and optimization strategies for line styles and compressed display lists will serve as a valuable resource for the wider map rendering community. To enhance the capabilities of sequence modeling networks in addressing long sequences, dual-path RNNs were previously proposed by dividing long sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with corresponding sub-networks for partial and full modeling, resulting in dual-path RNNs. We have now applied this concept to complex neural speech separation models by developing a dual-path RNN encoder, which significantly simplifies the sequence modeling responsibility for the encoder and allows the attention mechanism to focus on partial modeling for both the source and target speech. Compared to a straightforward approach using a single sequence model for both speech streams, the dual-path RNN encoder separation model yields a notable reduction in parameters and training time while achieving comparable or improved speech separation performance. Experimental evaluations conducted on the WSJ0 speech separation dataset have demonstrated the effectiveness of this model. Additionally, the code developed for this research is now publicly accessible.

We investigate the impact of radius definitions including event, apparent, and ergoscreen radii on the analysis of thermodynamic phase transitions within rotating black holes in an asymptotically flat spacetime. Due to the presence of gravitationally distorted surroundings in real astrophysical black hole observations, determining the true radius through holography is crucial. We analyze the distinct behaviors of the heat capacity and the free energy of the rotating black hole in both its inner and outer regions in order to better understand phase transitions and various radius definitions. Our research reveals that considering only the event horizon radius might lead to misinterpretations of heat capacity and the van der Waals-like phase transition equation of state. Additionally, we discuss the possible applications and limitations of our findings to non-rotating and charged black holes. Our results highlight the significance of accurately defining radius in calculating heat capacity and the free energy of black holes, thereby affecting our understanding of phase transitions. Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances. Our findings highlight the potential of combining state-of-the-art measurement techniques with free-choice detection settings to accommodate various quantum applications, depending on the specific properties of the generated state of light. Additionally, we show that the Wigner function can be effectively obtained from the optical tomogram by applying a specific inverse operation through a spatial or temporal transformation of the detected field, depending on the detection setting used. Ultimately, our research shows that optical tomography offers a high degree of flexibility, allowing for balanced trade-offs between state reconstruction complexity and practical feasibility in quantum experiments. Our results also provide visual evidence for the unique spatial or temporal signatures corresponding to distinct non-classical effects in Michelson-like setups, featuring death valley structures in the optical tomogram associated with entanglement generation, which could be valuable for educating students about these phenomena through visualization. Finally, we demonstrate the practical applicability of our findings by successfully reconstructing the Wigner function from experimental optical tomograms obtained using a detection setup with variable settings, demonstrating the utility of our approach for post-processing data from state preparation experiments. Our proposed method is suitable for generating the Wigner function from optical tomograms obtained behind a beam splitter in both its linear and nonlinear regime, as well as for experiments involving two-photon states behind a type II optical parametric oscillator, leading to a deeper understanding of the relationship between the optical tomograms and the Wigner function, especially in complex scenarios involving intermediate detection settings and varying initial states of the radiation field. Our research provides a versatile state reconstruction approach that can be adapted for use in a wide range of experiments and beam configurations, offering valuable insights into the relationship between the optical tomograms and the Wigner function, particularly in situations with multiple output ports and varying initial states of the radiation field. However, the current streaming technology faces challenges in delivering smooth and high-quality 360-degree video services due to the enormous data requirements and limited bandwidth. A novel video streaming approach is proposed to address this issue by developing a 360-degree video streaming framework that incorporates a novel point-of-interest (POI)-based 360-degree video encoding technique and a dynamic streaming strategy. In the encoding phase, the proposed framework prioritizes and encodes the most important viewing areas to minimize data loss, while the streaming phase adapts to changing user preferences and network conditions to optimize the streaming process. Experimental results show that the proposed framework achieves a significant reduction in encoded data loss and an improvement in streaming stability and continuity. Evaluations with real users indicate that the proposed framework yields higher ratings for visual quality, streaming continuity, and overall satisfaction compared to conventional streaming methods. The impact of infrared renormalons in the color dipole gluon distribution's variance is being quantified, and calculations demonstrate how non-linear small-x saturation impacts shift the Borel plane's initial IR pole from $2/\beta_2$ to $1/\beta_2$, thereby altering the estimate for the first infrared renormalon to $1/(N_f \cdot C_A)$ from $1/(N_f \cdot 2 \cdot C_A)$. As a result, the estimated scale for the infrared component in the variance transitions from $\sim 1/(N_f \cdot C_A)$ to $\sim 1/(N_f \cdot 2 \cdot C_A)$. The analysis also uncovers a complex pattern of poles along the $\beta_1$ axis in the Borel plane, leading to an estimated scale for the ultraviolet component in the variance as $\sim 4/\beta_1$ rather than $\sim 2/\beta_1$. The study's findings are relevant to recent measurements of deep inelastic scattering data and can be applied to similar future experiments with available data. The impact of infrared renormalons on the variance of the color tripole gluon distribution is also explored, along with the influence on the estimated scale components in both the deep inelastic scattering case and those involving proton-proton collisions at the LHC. The research provides an initial calculation for the variance of the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic generated by the color dipole gluon distribution, leading to an improved understanding of the estimated scale components in low-x physics. The impact of infrared renormalons on the variance of the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic is also examined in the context of proton-proton collisions at the LHC. The study's final section presents an assessment of its limitations and proposes potential avenues for further research, including the application of similar methods to other gluon distribution functions, the investigation of higher-order corrections to the Borel operator, and the development of a more advanced approximation than the stationary phase method for calculating the variance of the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, making it unsuitable for situations where only the original network's outputs are available. To overcome this limitation and make knowledge distillation more versatile, we develop a novel method called "output distillation", where we train a compact model using only the softened logits of a pre-trained network, without requiring the intermediate knowledge of the original model. We demonstrate that output distillation can achieve comparable performance to traditional knowledge distillation, with results showing that it successfully transfers knowledge from networks of different capacities and structures, including one that is significantly slower and has a much smaller capacity. Furthermore, output distillation is more computationally efficient than traditional knowledge distillation, as it doesn't need to transmit the softened labels between training and student models, thus enabling a more scalable solution for deep neural networks. System implementations are also provided for understanding the output distillation process in real-world scenarios. Source code is available at: https://github.com/zhanglei1993/output_distillation.

However, for modules that have no module composition multiplicities, we present an alternative approach based on the composition factors, drawing on the concept of strongly normal submodules. Specifically, for such modules, we demonstrate the steps to construct their lattice of submodules, beginning with their smallest and largest submodules, and including all strongly normal submodules as intermediate layers. Moreover, we validate our approach by applying this method to modules over the ring $\mathbb{Z}_2$, comparing the results with their respective lattices obtained through alternative methods, and including an analysis of the implications for non-abelian groups. Additionally, we provide an in-depth examination of the lattice structures for the submodules of the modules associated with these groups, including the Militades Monoid, the dihedral group $D_3$, the symmetric group $S_3$, and the quaternion group $Q_8$. Nonetheless, when considering modules over rings with module composition multiplicities, we show that the associated lattice structures lose their recognizability, failing to adhere to the Mal'cev tree pattern. When using an optimal metric function, the middle points in polar code variants can be skipped, as validated through simulations, leading to a substantial decrease in decoding computations with minimal compromise in error-correction performance. Moreover, an optimal threshold for convolutional codes is determined to ensure seamless integration between convolutional and polar code components, thereby maximizing the benefits of PAC codes. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the exceptional error-correction capabilities and computational efficiency of PAC codes, which can be seamlessly applied to various channel conditions. As a testament to the efficiency of PAC codes, with a code size of 512, they are able to achieve a block error rate of less than 10^-4 under a SNR of 2.2 dB for memoryless Gaussian channels. Additionally, our findings can be used as a blueprint for enhancing other sequential decoding schemes that incorporate PAC codes. Systematic and kernel PAC codes are also introduced in this paper, which enable further reductions in computations and code sizes, respectively. Consequently, our research significantly enhances the sequential decoding of channels with memory by polarizing convolutional codes, which remains a leading method for its unparalleled error-correction performance. Our work also reveals the minimum required memory and rate for PAC codes to function efficiently, which is inversely proportional to the code size and code rate, respectively. As a result, our research provides a promising solution for addressing the computational challenges faced by channels with memory in low-SNR scenarios. Neural machine translation systems often suffer from low reinforcement learning effectiveness when using word-level rewards, a issue that becomes particularly problematic when the vocabulary is reduced due to training data limitations or style-based filtering. We propose an alternative approach, titled selective output generation, which focuses on producing a limited vocabulary that is most relevant for machine translation. By reducing the output vocabulary to a size that enhances reinforcement learning's effectiveness, we achieve significant improvements in translation quality, as measured by both BLEU scores and human evaluations. Our approach surpasses the current reinforcement learning norms for neural machine translation and establishes a new baseline for future research. Our method is straightforward to implement and does not require any additional training data beyond the standard translation training corpus. We also introduce a new REINFORCE algorithm that mitigates the vanishing gradient issue caused by large action values in the output vocabulary. Our findings are backed by comprehensive corpus-based evaluations and human assessments of both automatic summarization and machine translation systems. Systems that generate text according to a given style or set of constraints have an inherent problem - evaluating their performance. Since there are no reference texts available for comparison, researchers rely on intrinsic metrics like coherence scores or human evaluations. However, these methods are costly and do not account for the underlying semantics of the text. In contrast, extrinsic evaluation assesses a text generation system's ability to effectively use its generated text in a downstream task. Following this idea, we propose a novel metric based on reinforcement learning that measures a text generation system's ability to effectively produce relevant words when constrained by a limited vocabulary. We further constrain the system to a word vocabulary where only a subset of the total vocabulary is allowed, making the system more efficient at generating relevant words

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, along with formal specifications using Lamport's temporal logic. We also established what levels of atomicity and isolation are achieved by MongoDB transactions, based on standard definitions and using the STARSE specification framework. Finally, we used our pseudocode and formal specifications to create executable models of MongoDB's transactional protocols for the TLA+ validation tool, which can be used for further verification and testing. Our effort provides a transparent and verifiable understanding of MongoDB's transactional protocols. We also believe that our approach could be applied to other distributed databases that offer transactions. Our execution models and verification environments are available at https://github.com/DBsLab/MongoDB-Transactions. We plan to update them whenever the MongoDB database is updated. We recommend that database administrators and developers verify the consistency of MongoDB's transactional protocols for themselves, given the importance of this verification for their respective work. Research in condensed matter physics is driven by the goal of fully understanding and characterizing complex and intriguing phenomena associated with geometric frustration. Frustration arises when the tendencies of individual components within a system clash due to its constrained structure, prompting an in-depth examination of how it influences the behavior of local spin probes in mesoscopic systems. This review focuses on the spin systems exhibiting the most fascinating and previously misunderstood phenomena, including Kitaev's honeycomb model and spin-1 lifshitz point material, and delves into the theoretical and experimental methods used to study their microphysical structures and dynamics. Various techniques such as neutron scattering and NMR are explored and representative examples of spin-1 lifshitz point material and Kitaev's honeycomb model are studied through both theoretical and experimental lenses, highlighting the intricate balance between competing orders and the difficulties in accurately interpreting data in search of distinctive signatures of competing states of order. Despite these challenges, researchers have made notable progress in recent years, including the discovery of stripe phase order in spin-1 lifshitz point material and the detection of individual components of order in Kitaev's honeycomb model, paving the way for future breakthroughs in understanding the behavior of spin systems driven by geometric frustration.

This review also delves into the experimental techniques used to study these systems, including neutron scattering and NMR, which have been instrumental in advancing the understanding of these systems. Ultimately, the study of these systems has revealed the intricate relationship between competing orders and the environments in which they thrive, as well as the challenges posed by achieving a precise understanding of these complex systems. This knowledge has far-reaching implications for the development of new materials with unique properties that arise from the interplay of competing orders. This review is part of a special issue on non-equilibrium dynamics and competing orders

We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Calculating the energy flux as the square of the sum of the products of each particle type's energy, density, and the speed of light, we found an average energy flux of about 69 Watts per square meter at a distance of one solar radius from the solar center, which is remarkably consistent with models of the solar wind and does not require any assumptions about the conditions at the solar surface. Nonetheless, the accuracy of speech-emotion recognition in real-world situations remains an area of improvement. A major limitation of existing methods is their inability to adapt models to new domains seamlessly. In this research, a innovative technique is developed to effortlessly transfer a speech-emotion recognition model from a synthetic or controlled dataset to any real-world setting. The system utilizes a domain-adaptable model to interpret the subtle nuances of audio signals and another task-specific model to identify emotions in audio. The model's ability to function across different domains is ensured by minimizing the distance between the adapted representations of domain samples. Through rigorous testing on three publicly available datasets, the system demonstrated an impressive capacity to adapt to new domains with minimal effort. In particular, the system achieved a notable 11.1% boost in the accuracy of speech-emotion recognition in a publicly available dataset used in singing emotion recognition tasks. In addition, the system showed remarkable performance in adapting to new domains with just 1 hour of live data. The system's efficacy is further highlighted by comparing it with alternative domain adaptation techniques widely used in speech-emotion recognition research, including the popular adversarial domain adaptation method. In conclusion, the system developed in this research offers a cutting-edge solution for speech-emotion recognition research in real-world settings with limited data. Researchers studying strong shock waves in an expanding universe have found similar results using both approximate analytical and exact numerical methods to solve self-similar equations. When the adiabatic index lies between one and approximately 1.16, these solutions consistently occupy all available fluid and void spaces, showing no intermediate state. As the index surpasses this threshold, pressure and density begin to vary significantly, with multiple discontinuities emerging within the fluid region. These shocks can also exert a substantial gravitational influence on their surrounding space. Additionally, analysis has shown that even weak shocks eventually grow and merge with other shocks, gaining sufficient power to impact the universe's overall structure. These findings are also applicable to multiple-dimensional scenarios beyond one-dimensional models. The analysis of these solutions also includes the breakdown of self-similar descriptions in two-dimensional expanding universes. The role of entropy fluctuations in one-dimensional scenarios is also examined, with results demonstrating their ability to influence the index but not the overall shock wave behavior. The discussion of these solutions is set within the broader context of expanding universes and the breakdown of self-similar descriptions. Building on previous work by Freeman and Shea-Bahnhof, along with others, we modify their approach to effectively handle a wide range of scale separations between high and low estimates of a trajectory. The significance of this research is underscored by the fact that many real-world systems exhibit chaotic behavior on multiple scales, yet the theory behind their analysis has struggled to keep pace, thanks in part to the difficulty it poses for the algorithm to produce geophysically plausible results. Nevertheless, with our new algorithm, we have successfully applied this technique to a notable example of such a system - the atmosphere - using a representative location to obtain a dynamics correlation spectrum that provides additional insight into the underlying dynamics. Despite the atmosphere's behavior being complex and difficult to model, our findings indicate that our algorithm is capable of uncovering the essence of these dynamics with just a single location's data, whereas more traditional methods require the combination of data from multiple locations to achieve the same level of understanding. Furthermore, our research reveals that the algorithm is highly effective even when the scale of the high estimate is extremely small in comparison to the low estimate, which is a common occurrence in many natural settings, though it does necessitate the use of the algorithm with caution to avoid any potential misinterpretation of the resulting correlation dimension spectra. Ultimately, our new algorithm offers a valuable tool for the analysis of complex dynamics within natural settings, along with providing concrete evidence of the atmosphere's chaotic behavior on a global scale, as demonstrated by the distinctive shape of the correlation dimension spectrum that we have termed the 'eye of the hurricane diagram'. This phenomenon is particularly notable when analyzing the dynamics within the eye of a hurricane, where the algorithm uncovers a previously unreported level of detail that is characterized by four distinct scales of self-similarity - two that are fractal in nature and two that are non-fractal. Consequently, our research has significant implications for our understanding of the atmosphere's behavior, especially within the context of tropical cyclones, though its applicability is not limited to just this specific setting. The Yang-Mills-aether theory is analyzed to understand the implications of introducing non-abelian aether-like terms that violate Lorentz symmetry, specifically within thermal quantum field theory. By incorporating temperature effects and spatial compactification via Thermofield Dynamics, corrections to the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law and non-abelian Casimir energy and pressure are calculated for both zero and finite temperatures. Furthermore, a distinction is drawn between the non-abelian and abelian scenarios in the Casimir effect. The non-abelian Yang-Mills-aether scenario is found to induce a negative energy density in both zero and finite temperature settings, whereas a positive energy density emerges in the abelian setting only at finite temperatures. The non-abelian Yang-Mills-aether theory's energy density and pressure differences exhibit a temperature-dependent behavior, displaying an abrupt transition from lower to higher temperatures. This transition's hysteresis is attributed to the non-abelian nature of the theory. The energy density and pressure differences are found to be proportional to the square of the coupling constant, whereas the abelian scenario shows a decoupling effect. The non-abelian Yang-Mills-aether theory's predictions are found to result in the non-abelian theory's energy and pressure differences eventually becoming negative, leading to an instability in both zero and finite temperature settings. The implications of these findings for non-abelian Yang-Mills-aether theory are discussed, as are potential future research directions. The models developed in this research can also serve as effective theories for more comprehensive, fundamentally motivated extensions of quantum field theory that incorporate temperature and spatial compactification effects. The method employed in this research can be applied to other non-abelian gauge theories with aether-like terms. The research in this paper also contributes to the broader study of quantum field theory in curved spacetime, focusing on the thermal aspects of non-abelian Yang-Mills-aether theory. The thermal aspects of non-abelian Yang-Mills-aether theory are explored in detail, providing a foundation for future studies on the subject. The calculation methods developed in this research can be applied to the study of thermal aspects in other non-abelian gauge theories with aether-like terms. The paper also presents a compactification of non-abelian Yang-Mills-aether theory in the context of Thermofield Dynamics, serving as a starting point for future studies on the subject. The research in this paper can be seen as an extension of previous studies on the Casimir effect

This research develops a method for estimating the expected cost of hedging European options through the delta-hedging process, resulting in a computationally efficient formula that accounts for option prices and the behavior of delta processes. Initially, a standard unit hedging cost is established and subsequently, the total hedging cost is determined as the product of this unit cost, stock price, a supply curve factor, and the square of the number of options. Consequently, this formulation enables faster computation of expected hedging costs than alternative Monte Carlo methods. The study also provides explicit numerical examples to demonstrate the practical applications of this method in specific contexts. Moreover, the research is expandable to accommodate more complex models, including stochastic volatility and jump processes. Ultimately, this work can be integrated with existing risk management frameworks to provide a fast and accurate calculation of hedging costs, thereby enhancing existing strategies to accommodate hedging costs in the delta process. This can be achieved by simply adding the hedging cost factor to the risk-free rate in the underlying stochastic process used to value options. This approach has already been validated in the literature for the risk-free rate, and by extension, it can be applied to the hedging cost factor as well. This enables the valuation of hedging costs to be seamlessly incorporated into existing models and risk management frameworks, thereby providing a more comprehensive and nuanced understanding of the value of hedging costs in the context of option valuation. A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across 
generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To 
investigate this dynamic in South Korea, a society characterized by strong social 
mobility ties, our research examines the underlying factors contributing to mobility 
within its social class structure. By using detailed family and educational data from 
tax records and university admission information, we reconstructed the educational paths 
of nearly an million South Koreans born between 1955 and 1979. The findings from 
these detailed educational histories reveal the diverse routes individuals take to 
attain higher education, influenced by factors such as family background, economic 
status, and educational opportunities available to them. Consequently, we developed 
methods to calculate the chances of individuals moving up a social class based on 
their own educational experiences and those of their parents. By applying these 
methods to the reconstructed educational histories, we gathered comprehensive data on 
social mobility in South Korea across multiple generations. The results show that, 
despite having strong social mobility ties, South Korea experiences significant 
obstacles to social mobility, particularly when looking at the 30-year period from 1979 
to 2009. During this time, the chances of moving up a social class by obtaining a 
higher education declined by 15 percentage points, primarily due to the limited 
opportunities available to lower social class families to send their children to 
universities. When examining the dynamics of social mobility within the lower 
social class category, our research reveals a disturbing pattern of persistent 
social immobility across generations in South Korea. If an individual from a lower 
social class fails to attain higher education, there is a 79% chance that they will 
remain in the same social class for the next 30 years, highlighting the lasting 
impact of social class on an individual's and their descendants' socioeconomic status. 
Our research underlines the significance of equal access to education as a means of 
breaking free from the constraints of social class, a concept particularly pertinent 
in South Korea where social mobility across generations is heavily influenced by 
educational opportunities available to individuals and their families. Our data and 
analysis provide a unique perspective on social mobility in South Korea and its 
dynamics, a topic that has been extensively studied in other developed economies. Our 
methodological approach to measuring social mobility is also innovative as we use

Furthermore, they provided critical input for future luminosity upgrades, given the significant impact of beam optics on future luminosity limits. The successful implementation and data analysis presented in this paper serve as a foundation for future beam physics studies at the LHC, particularly in the context of future luminosity upgrades, such as High-Luminosity and Future Circular Colliders. The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. This paper presents a Python tool,'s4cmb', which generates simulated raw data streams in the time domain for contemporary cosmic microwave background experiments based on bolometric technology. The package also includes a suite of tools to calculate instrumental systematic effects and simulate noisy data in the frequency domain. This should enable more realistic and comprehensive instrumental systematic effect estimates and facilitate more accurate calculations of achievable sensitivities for future experiments. The code is designed to be highly flexible, allowing users to easily modify their own setups using the same framework used in the development. The tool is hosted on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/cosmicmx/s4cmb. The accompanying documentation is available at the following address: https://s4cmb.readthedocs.io/en/latest/. The tool has been tested on representative examples of current and future cosmic microwave background experiments, including the Tomsk State University's Bantay experiment, the QUBT experiment located in Nainital, India, and the next-generation CMB experiment, the Primus experiment based in Chile. The code can be modified to accommodate other types of detectors and experiments with similar bolometric technology. The simulation of raw data streams and subsequent frequency domain data is accompanied by example analyses of the simulated data streams and frequency domain data. These examples cover calculations of achievable sensitivities and estimations of achievable noise levels in the beam window function. The code's design allows users to easily incorporate their own specific analysis tools into the package. The tool's framework is highly flexible and can be easily adapted for the simulation of other types of experiments with similar detector technology. The code is compatible with commonly used operating systems including Linux and MacOS, although it may not be compatible with Windows due to the use of specific command-line interfaces. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of metric spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of proximal metric spaces. This article aims to extend upon Menger's initial problems by incorporating spaces with angle functions, resulting in the publication's main contribution. Furthermore, the article provides a distinct solution to one of these problems, effectively generalizing the approach previously developed for metric spaces by U. Bessaga and A. Pelczynski in 1958. Additionally, the article presents a relationship between spaces with angle functions and the structure of semi-metric spaces, serving as a natural framework for defining these spaces. The article also explores specific examples of spaces with angle functions, demonstrating how they compare to known geometric domains, including the Euclidean space, the hyperbolic plane, and the metric spaces associated with certain random geometric domains. The article's main theorem establishes that, when the angle function satisfies a specific condition, it is possible to define a compatible semi-metric on the underlying set, providing a means to investigate the topological properties of these spaces. The article also presents an application of this theorem to demonstrate how spaces with angle functions can be embedded into the structure of semi-metric spaces, effectively generalizing the approach previously developed for proximal metric spaces by J. Hagelstein and A. Berman in 1979. The article's final section explores research directions related to spaces with angle functions, including potential applications to domains with corners and polynomial domains, as well as spaces with angle functions defined on countable state Markov decision processes. The article's main contribution also extends upon the recent publication by the third-listed authors, A. Berman and J. Hagelstein, from 1989, regarding the dynamic nature of spaces with angle functions in the context of these state spaces, though with a focus on discrete time intervals. The article's final section explores how the introduction of a condition on the angle function's rate of change can influence the topology of these spaces, as well as how this comparison applies to the Euclidean space, the hyperbolic plane, and the metric spaces associated with certain random geometric domains. The article's main theorem also provides a means to investigate the topological properties of these dynamic spaces, as well as how they evolve

We introduce a rigid cluster model to achieve a representation of the quantum group U_q(g) for Lie algebras of type ADE. This involves establishing a natural isomorphism from the quantum group U_q(g) to a subalgebra within the quotient of Weyl group invariants from the Fock-Goncharov quantum cluster algebra O_q(P_G ∘). Leveraging the quantum duality of cluster algebras, we find that U_q(g) possesses a natural basis \bar{Θ} whose structural coefficients consist of non-negative integers in the variable set {q^(1/2), q^(-1/2)}. Furthermore, the basis \bar{Θ} maintains an invariance property under the braid group action defined by Lusztig, Dynkin's automorphisms, and the star anti-involution. Additionally, the basis \bar{Θ} contains the quantum integers \bar{θ} as a subbasis, enabling the extension of U_q(g) to a range of q-values, thereby retrieving the original basis Θ generated by E_i / ∆_i. Ultimately, this allows us to demonstrate that the quantum group U_q(g) retains its original properties within the extended range of q-values. Moreover, we establish that the quantum Weyl group W_q retains its full group structure within the extended range of q-values. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking members who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded participants. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an in-depth analysis of a well-established and widespread pyramid scam, Dunya Invest, by exploring the financial connections among its members and the broader global network of associated accounts. A deep dive into account relationships was achieved through the application of a combined approach combining machine learning algorithms and graph theory. This method allowed for the identification of pyramid tiers and a review of transaction patterns among members. In addition, IP addresses associated with servers hosting control panels were used to map the network of participants and servers. A review of transaction patterns and the geographical distribution of participants and associated servers shed light on the scheme's operators and their primary means of recruiting new members and generating profits for existing members. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the feasibility of scrutinizing a sophisticated pyramid scam like Dunya Invest through the application of advanced network analysis techniques. This approach provides a detailed understanding of the underlying network of a pyramid scam, its operator's recruitment strategies, and the geographic reach of its associated servers and participants. This type of analysis can be invaluable for regulatory bodies and financial institutions in their efforts to combat investment scams. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete, as indicated by the observed asymmetry in the distribution of clusters within the bulge. We have made a comprehensive search for missing globular clusters within the bulge, focusing on likely cluster candidates that have been previously overlooked. Using high-quality near-infrared color-excess maps, we have estimated the normal and total extinction ranges for the known and candidate globular clusters within the bulge, which range from 1.0 to 2.5 times the interstellar medium. We have also calculated the likely reddening and extinction ranges for the bulge clusters based on the intrinsic colors of stars within these clusters. We have found that the current catalog of globular clusters undercounts the total number of clusters within the bulge by a factor of two, with the majority of these clusters being small, distant, and heavily extincted. We have identified 16 new globular cluster candidates within the bulge, which were discovered by analyzing high-resolution images of the bulge region, specifically the $[x, y, $\sigma$]$ maps of the bulge. We have applied a set of criteria to these maps, which prioritize clusters with distinct cores, high central density, and cluster members within the half-light radius, in order to ensure that only genuine cluster candidates are included in the catalog. We have estimated the parameters of these 16 new candidates, which are likely to become confirmed globular clusters once they are observed with high-resolution spectroscopy, including their distance, total mass, absolute magnitude, mass function, and metallicity. We have further divided the bulge clusters into two distinct populations, the classical and young, based on their metallicity, which is reflected in their color and distance. We have found that the search area within the bulge is divided into two distinct regions, with a significant gap in cluster density at a longitude of $-10^\circ$, which corresponds to the bar-bulge transition region. We have also found that the distribution of clusters within the bulge is highly asymmetrical, with a significant shortage of clusters within the southern region of the bulge, which we believe may indicate a shortage of clusters within the Galactic disk that surrounds the bulge. We have further searched for the Sgr dSph cluster candidates within the Sgr stream, which we have found may be composed of two distinct populations, the old and young, with a significant gap in mass between the two populations. We have estimated the mass of the Sgr dSph cluster population

Our analysis reveals that the class of holographic codes, which include the Haah's cubic code, can be effectively represented using tensor networks that possess certain architectural features. Specifically, these codes and networks must satisfy specific conditions, including being designed to withstand erasure decoding and exhibiting distinct, distinct phases in their bifurcations. When these conditions are met, we demonstrate that a unified, error-correcting framework can be applied to both the cubic code and its network representation, yielding a unified, error-correcting framework that can be applied to both. Additionally, our analysis highlights the differences between the cubic code and other codes, including Haah's shallow code, which the cubic code can be compared to. Finally, we also investigate the relationship between the Haah's cubic code and the Haah's shallow code, demonstrating that they can both be integrated into a single, comprehensive framework of holographic codes. This framework encompasses both the cubic code and the shallow code, revealing that the shallow code can be considered a sub-class of the cubic code, along with revealing that the cubic code itself can be viewed as a modification of the shallow code, involving the incorporation of additional redundancy. This framework also provides a holistic understanding of the distinctive characteristics that the cubic code possesses, including its unique structure, its decoding capabilities, as well as its specific phase transitions, which together define its distinct identity within the broader category of holographic codes. We investigate key properties of the Gelfand-Shilov spaces ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$, which are characterized by their rapid decay and smoothness requirements. The nontriviality of these spaces, defined as having an infinite-dimensional set of analytic characters, is shown to occur when the space's parameters satisfy certain ratios. This research also explores relationships between ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$ and the Roumier spaces ${\Gamma}^{\sigma}_s$, as well as testing their properties through the analysis of partial differential equations involving Toeplitz operators. Furthermore, new results regarding the invertibility of these operators are established, and associated microlocal analysis is examined. The connection between the spaces' parameters and the operator's invertibility is crucial for solving problems related to the propagation of singularities and partial differential equations on the spaces ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$. The study presented here serves as a foundation for future research aimed at applying these spaces and associated operators to microlocal analysis. Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method, achieving superior performance compared to existing GAN-based models. Additionally, the model's representational capabilities are shown to be comparable to those of high-performance neural text generation models, despite its relatively simple architecture. System evaluations further highlight the generative capabilities of SparseGAN, yielding generated texts with comparable grammatical correctness and substantially improved semantic similarity when compared to existing GAN-based models. To facilitate reproducibility, the code for SparseGAN is available at this link https://github.com/zhongjie116/SparseGAN. To facilitate further research, two evaluation metrics for generated texts are introduced and made publicly available on the Web: a automatic assessment tool at this link https://github.com/zhongjie116/SentSim and a human evaluation platform at this link https://gan-eval.com/. To facilitate model deployment, the SparseGAN model can be obtained from this link https://github.com/zhongjie116/SparseGAN. The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past. Although interstellar panspermia is an engaging theory, it's incredibly difficult to verify this hypothesis through observation, as any evidence from a previous system would likely be erased by the current one. A new hypothesis is proposed, centered on the assumption that life on a planet is influenced by a lack of long-term stability within its system, as seen through the orbit of a planet within a highly eccentric habitable zone. This theory can be tested by analyzing future telescopic data from planetary microlensing observations, which can reveal the prevalence of life on planets with varying orbital periods, even if those planets are no longer habitable today. According to our model, a planet would exhibit signs of life through a specific pattern of oxygen production if it falls within a particular distance from its star, a range that can be determined through microlensing observations, even after a planet has left the habitable zone. Although future telescopic technology might be able to detect oxygen directly from exoplanets, a large-scale survey of a significant portion of the Milky Way is required to observe the spread of life on a planetary scale, which could provide clear evidence of interstellar panspermia. However, even then, there would be an alternative explanation based on the distribution of planetary orbits and the formation of star clusters. Nevertheless, detecting the spread of life on a planetary scale could also provide a direct link to another engaging hypothesis known as the interstellar recycling of life. While it's difficult to test the latter hypothesis through observation, it's an appealing concept that could give new meaning to the idea that life on Earth originated from comets. Although comets are now seen as a source of organic compounds rather than life itself, it's possible that a more exotic explanation for the origins of life on Earth is yet to be discovered, an explanation that could be revealed through future telescopic observations of exoplanetary atmospheres. As such, we propose a new hypothesis centered on the recycling of life, which could be tested by analyzing future data from telescopic observations of exoplanetary atmospheres, data that could give a new and unexpected answer to one of the most enduring questions in science, a question that has been debated for centuries, ever since the time of Epicurus. Animal population research is facing an era of heightened accountability where
decisions made by managers are guided by data-driven choices.  A persistent
challenge hindering the widespread use of animal population data in decision
making relates to inadequate knowledge of their spatial use patterns across their
entire habitats.  A valuable tool for discovering these hidden patterns is the
resource selection function (RSF), a linear model that predicts probability of
use (PU) at unsampled locations.  However, estimating PU values at all points
in a habitat, including those outside of a study area, is difficult due to the
need for accurate extrapolation beyond the geographical boundaries defined by
data sets.  A novel nonparametric method is proposed to enhance the predictive
accuracy of PU values beyond the limits of their original data sources.  This
approach, known as spatial bridge, leverages data sets from other locations to
refine the RSF models created from others, allowing for the successful
extrapolation of PU values to areas outside of their respective data bases.
Advantages of this approach include facilitating data sharing and allowing
the use of publicly available data sets from other researchers.  A simulated study
and a real world example demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in
predicting PU values with a high degree of accuracy, especially in areas beyond
the limits of their original data bases.  This method levers multiple source
data sets to create individual site level PU values, which can be aggregated to
estimate habitat level PU values, thus providing a practical solution for
managing large habitats based on data from smaller ones.  This method is simple,  data-efficient and highly transferable with wide applicability in animal population research and management.  A key assumption of this approach is that there are sufficient spatial bridges available for all habitats of interest.  A tool to support this approach is also provided, along with the method's code and future research directions.  This work has implications for various fields including ecology, geography, and wildlife management. The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various dynamic systems that evolve across different time frames. In contrast to single-layer networks, multilayer networks can capture the co-evolution of multiple dynamics layers by applying non-parametric Bayesian methods. This study extends the concept further to multilayer networks with time-varying parameters and changing topological relationships, enabling the incorporation of exogenous inputs that influence the system's dynamics. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to a multilayer network featuring co-evolving topology and dynamics, specifically the spread of infectious diseases represented by the SIR model. By comparing it to a model that assumes time-invariant parameters and static network topology, our research shows that models with time-variant parameters and changing network topologies better capture the complex dynamics of real systems, leading to more accurate predictions and better performance in controlling the system. System control is achieved through the incorporation of external inputs that influence the system's dynamics and network topology in a way that prioritizes stability above all else. Our research tool is implemented using the Network-X and PyDynamic libraries in Python. Our findings are supported by numerical results obtained from simulated data available for public use, namely the data related to the 2009 A/H1N1 pandemic in the city of Zurich. Our code is available at this link https://github.com/IntelligentSystemLab/Application-of-Bayesian-Methods-in-Network-Dynamics. The benefits of multilayer networks become particularly apparent when analyzing systems that exhibit different dynamics across various time frames, such as seasonal patterns in temperature or the spread of influenza and other contagious diseases. In these cases, models that capture the co-evolution of multiple dynamics layers over time may offer significant advantages over single-layer networks by allowing for the non-parametric estimation of time-varying network topologies and system dynamics using Bayesian methods. Our research built upon this concept by extending existing models to accommodate changing network topologies and time-varying parameters, which were particularly useful in simulating and analyzing the spread of the SIR model in a network. By comparing it to a more restrictive model with time-invariant parameters and static network topology, our research demonstrated the benefits of extended models in mirroring real-world dynamics more accurately, which in turn led to enhanced performance in predicting and controlling the system. System control was achieved by incorporating external inputs that influenced the system's dynamics and network topology in a way that prioritized stability above all else. Our research tool was developed using the Network-X and PyDynamic libraries in Python.

Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating differential equation from input and output data can be seen as an inverse problem for the operator. This process is made more manageable by the introduction of a modified stress operator, which enables the creation of a virtual system and facilitates the derivation of necessary and sufficient conditions for the operator to be considered as the generator of a differential equation meeting specific requirements. These requirements include the absence of non-causal components, the presence of a well-defined degree, and adherence to a specific differential order. A practical method for determining the order of the differential operator is also presented, alongside a proposal for distinguishing between irreducible and non-irreducible operators. A workable approach for solving inverse problems is demonstrated through a specific numerical example, showing that the associated differential operator can be recovered using a virtual system and its associated stress operator. This approach is found to be effective even when solving a differential flatness order determination problem in a nonlinear optimal control scenario. In such a case, the operator is initially estimated and then refined through an iterative process. This approach is found to result in a significant improvement in the response time of the system being controlled. In contrast to the standard approach, it does not require the initial guess of the order of the differential operator and is thus considered a more robust method. In addition to its applications in the fields of control and signal processing, this approach also has implications for the study of partial differential equations. In particular, it provides a geometrically justified basis for the use of gradient descent algorithms in the solution of certain PDEs. Similarly, it offers a differential operator perspective on the inverse problem of recovering an unknown domain from partial information, a problem with applications in the fields of physics and biology. To analyze and manage traffic effectively, accurate traffic flow theory is essential.
This study applies the Gamma distribution to model queues in a traffic environment
with limited data, and further develops a Bayesian framework to estimate parameters
using limited probe vehicle information.
We first establish the relationship between queue length and travel time through Gamma
distribution properties, and then develop a Bayesian algorithm to estimate distribution
parameters using partial data from probe vehicles.
The algorithm is applied to estimated travel times from Google Maps, and the results
are validated by comparing simulated travel times with estimated parameters.
The study also compares estimated queue lengths using the Gamma distribution with those
from traditional methods, and finds that the Gamma distribution provides more accurate
results, especially during rush hour.
In addition, we extract relevant information from probe vehicle data, and compare
the accuracy of different sampling methods for reducing data, with the aim of
improving existing traffic management systems that can be enhanced by combining
predictive models and real-time data. The ultimate goal of this research is
to create a predictive model of queue lengths that can be used to develop optimal
traffic signal control systems, and to evaluate the effectiveness of different
management policies on reducing queue lengths and improving network efficiency. System performance metrics, including stop rate and travel time, will be used to assess the impact of different policies and system configurations on traffic networks. The study will also explore methods to integrate public transportation with private vehicles to improve network efficiency, reduce congestion, and decrease queue lengths. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by first applying the Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition to the traceless part of the extrinsic curvature, then solving the Hamiltonian constraint for the conformal scale factor, and finally solving the momentum constraints for the conformal tensor of the matter field. This method allows for initial data with conformally positive scalar curvatures and has been effectively used in simulations of binary neutron star mergers and rotating black hole neutron star systems. In particular, it has been found that solving the Hamiltonian constraint for the conformal scale factor factor after applying the Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition helps to reduce the negative eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian operator and associated conformal factor eigenvalue spectrum problems. As a result, this method yields well-posed initial data with a larger minimum allowed Bondi mass parameter than the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition approach. This method also provides a more accurate representation of the gravitational wave polarizations, which is crucial for achieving the desired accuracy in post-Newtonian simulations of binary neutron star mergers. This approach has been successfully applied in the $f$-diagonal gauge and has given rise to a well-behaved and smooth initial data geometry with a clear separation between the two merging bodies. This method is particularly beneficial for simulations of binary neutron star mergers with small mass asymmetry, where the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition approach may yield a negative Bondi mass parameter and fail to produce reliable post-merger oscillation waveforms. This approach has been utilized in the simulation of binary neutron star mergers with total masses ranging from 2.75 M_\\odot to 4.0 M_\\odot and mass ratios ranging from 0.25 to 0.75 in the rotating frame, where the merger occurs within 500-1500 ms after the start of the simulation. This method has been found to be highly effective in producing reliable post-merger oscillation waveforms with a wide range of mass ratios and in simulating black hole neutron star systems with small mass asymmetry. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic and magnetic structure, and the anomalous Hall effect within these materials remains poorly understood. We investigated the anomalous Hall effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskites from the TaGdTa and GdTaGd interfaces of a Ta/Gd/Ta trilayer, as changes in the interface studied significantly affect the spin and orbital moments of Gd. By analyzing the magnetic moment distribution and local environment, we found that only a small portion of Gd atoms contribute to the anomalous Hall effect, and these are confined to specific interface regions with particular atomic layers, where the spin-orbit coupling is more pronounced. We also found that the spin-orbit coupling at these interfaces is insufficient to generate the anomalous Hall effect on its own, and an interplay between spin, orbital, and magnetic moments is necessary for this effect to occur. Additionally, we found that the interfacial regions retain their magnetic moment distribution when heated to high temperatures, and as such, they may serve as robust, thermally stable platforms for manipulating the anomalous Hall effect. Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, the focus was on upper-limb function, but recent studies have shifted towards lower-limb recovery, specifically walking. Although successful, current methods require expensive and sophisticated equipment, limiting accessibility for many patients. To address this limitation, a novel, non-invasive BCI system for walking restoration was developed, utilizing a head-mounted camera to detect eye-gaze directions, which serve as inputs for a walking pattern generator. This system, unlike most existing techniques, does not require invasive electrodes or expensive gear, making it more patient-friendly and accessible in laboratory and clinical settings. Additionally, to enhance practical applicability, the system was tested on healthy individuals while they walked, demonstrating the safety and efficacy of the system. To validate its suitability for individuals with spinal cord injuries, the system was assessed on one such patient with partial thoracic spinal cord injury, showing that he could control the walking pattern using his eye-gaze directions, combined with electromyogram signals from his muscles. Consequently, this innovative, user-friendly BCI system offers promising results for recovering walking function in individuals with spinal cord injuries, providing a foundation for future research aimed at making the system more autonomous and capable of being used in the home environment. Human subjects were not involved in this study, as it was conducted in silico. A future study with real subjects is planned to validate the results obtained so far. In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification problems involving complex data structures. However, these approaches generally rely on static graph representations, which fail to capture the fundamental dynamics of changing connections crucial to understanding many real-world systems. We propose a novel neural network, called Temporal Graph Explorer Network (TGEN), that utilizes a Time-Embedding mechanism to dynamically learn node relationships at each time step, allowing for accurate classification of temporal graphs. We demonstrate TGEN's effectiveness by applying it to two classification tasks involving changing graph relationships: one based on hand-crafted features and another using a fully embedded scheme. Our method surpasses competing graph-based approaches in several respects, notably by circumventing the need to define distances between graphs and by dynamically capturing the evolving connectivity structure of systems over time. TGEN achieves superior performance in comparison to state-of-the-art methods, according to comprehensive evaluation metrics. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengzhong123/TGEN.

Animals move through their environments for various purposes such as foraging, escaping predators, and locating mating partners. The complexity of locomotion systems varies greatly across species with some animals employing highly intricate mechanisms like vertebrates' four-chambered hearts and four-legged skeletons. In contrast, many species like insects and worms utilize remarkably straightforward,'muscle-and-skeleton' based movements. Despite the diversity of locomotion systems, all share a common goal: moving with minimum energy expenditure while maintaining stability. This chapter will delve into the fundamental principles that underlie the stability and efficiency of locomotion, focusing on how animals adapt their gait to suit different situations and how simple models can effectively capture the essence of their movement patterns. The advent of big data has significant implications for scientific computation, prompting a shift towards creating highly scalable algorithms for matrix inversion. Developed for large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, the iterative algorithm known as Lightspeed uses a novel preconditioner in the matrix inversion context and has been implemented on the Intel KNL architecture. This study evaluates the optimized version of Lightspeed on Intel's NDR and XDR KNL architectures and compares its performance to other state-of-the-art methods, including PARDISO and ULITA, as well as the default and high-end Intel KNL architectures, revealing improved computation and memory efficiency. Specifically, Lightspeed achieves computation times and memory usage two times and three times smaller, respectively, than those of PARDISO and memory usage similar to ULITA. Furthermore, the research demonstrates how over-completion, node-level memory configuration, and architecture type influence computation time, with guidelines provided for optimizing Lightspeed performance. Ultimately, the results demonstrate the efficacy and scalability of Lightspeed, making it an appealing choice for matrix inversion applications, particularly those requiring low memory usage. The open-source Lightspeed code is accessible on GitHub. The research was conducted using the BigBrainGrid high-performance computing cluster, with the code developed in part using the GridGain high-performance computing framework. The study's findings are also applicable to other similar architectures, including Cray XC50 and ThinkScale TS140. The suitable problem size range for Lightspeed has been established as 10^6 to 10^7, depending on the architecture and memory available. The research demonstrates how Lightspeed's computation time can be two orders of magnitude faster than other methods for specific types of sparse matrix systems, particularly those with irregular structures, such as those encountered in the simulation of complex chemical reactions or certain types of image processing applications. The development of Lightspeed was supported in part by the National Science Foundation, with additional funding from Intel Corporation, as well as contributions from the Texas Advanced Computing Center and the University of Texas at Austin. We examine topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders. This study explores the effect of binary disorders on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings show that binary disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in multiple parameter ranges. This insulating phase is distinguished by the disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk modes in the sound-like mid-spectrum. Our research demonstrates that the topological phase boundaries of the unperturbed system serve as the core of the topological Anderson phases. We also investigate the effect of correlated disorders on zero-energy modes at disorder-averaged Bragg-like anticrossing structures. Our results demonstrate that the zero-energy mode's localization within the bulk or at the edges of the system depends on the disorder's amplitude and correlation length. This leads to the coexistence of edge states and the topological Anderson insulating phase in certain parameter ranges. Our work provides a detailed analysis of the factors influencing the magnitudes of the CP-odd and CP-even Higgs bosons and the resulting implications for their detection in various experiments. This surge is largely attributed to the development of decentralized solutions for context storage. In a notable recent contribution, a communication-efficient scheme for memoryless contextual linear bandits was established, utilizing approximately 5 dimensional bits per context. This achievement positioned its current record for the highest data efficiency achieved, surpassing previously set benchmarks by at least an order of magnitude. In this paper, we build upon this research by extending the context storage scheme to a fully decentralized setting, implementing a novel compression method based on a novel regression estimator, and combining multiple context storage solutions with varying effectiveness. Our results demonstrate an enhancement of the existing bound to approximately 5.3d bits per context, thereby solidifying the previous record with an margin of at least a magnitude of ten. This achievement is accomplished without the need for specific structural assumptions about the underlying system, making it universally applicable. In related work, we also examine the feasibility of extending this achievement to harder-to-solve problems, including contextual linear quadratic regulation and decentralized reinforcement learning. This work investigates the maximum allowable time to reach a perfectly balanced power distribution in a large wireless network, given its capacity constraints and the limited information available for user connections. The goal is to determine the optimal power allocation that maximizes network capacity while ensuring fairness among users, using recent developments in matrix theory. By leveraging the harmonic nature of optimal power scaling, we establish that the maximum gain achievable through power control is directly proportional to the square root of the total number of users. Additionally, we analyze the time required to reach a balanced power distribution and demonstrate that it can be as lengthy as squared many times the duration required for sufficient time to elapse for positive feedback protocols, although this time may be significantly reduced if the network allows for rapid feedback. The implications of these findings on current scheduling protocols are also considered, with potential applications in advanced networks incorporating relays and base stations. Numerical data confirming the efficacy of these protocols in realistic settings is provided through corresponding simulations. Legged robots can navigate a variety of environments, but controlling them on shifting, unstable ground poses a significant challenge. To effectively manage balance and movement, legged robots need accurate information about their surroundings and the ground they're standing on. Present control methods rely on simplified models of terrain behavior, which can lead to issues when dealing with complex, unpredictable ground conditions, such as those found in forest floors. To address this limitation, this research focuses on developing a control system that uses a detailed, realistic model of the terrain, specifically a deformable model based on the Biot-Geodesic formulation, in conjunction with an efficient simulation framework, dynamic multi-body dynamics, in a legged robot framework. By integrating this model into the robot's control system, it's possible to create a control strategy that takes into account the true dynamics of the terrain, leading to improved balance control and a significant reduction in energy expenditure. To achieve this, several optimizations were applied to enhance simulation efficiency, allowing for fast, accurate simulation of terrain deformation in real-time. Through a series of experiments and simulations, the effectiveness of this control system was demonstrated, showing that it could maintain balance more successfully and required less energy than traditional methods, even on unstable ground. To apply this method to actual robot movements, a prototype robot was created and experiments conducted among different terrain types, confirming the practical feasibility of this approach. To prepare for widespread use, the code developed during this research was incorporated into the OpenSimulator platform, a widely-used simulator platform. To further enhance the validity of future research, the code has been made accessible to the robotics community via the project webpage. To validate the accuracy of the simulations, comparisons were drawn with real-world measurements from the robot experiments, demonstrating the consistency between simulated and actual robot movements.
