Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. We prove that for nearly any random selection of a finite group's generating set, the diameter will be logarithmic in relation to the group's size, specifically with a specific constant of proportionality, which also applies to groups that have multiple distinct sets of generators. A direct application of this logarithmic proportionality can be seen in the following statement: for any given positive integer k, the majority of finite groups of size at least k will have a diameter of log_2(sup(k)), when considering groups of sizes ranging from k to infinity. A notable exception to this proportionality is seen with groups that have a large abelian subgroup of maximum rank, which can significantly exceed log_2(|G|) and thus can result in a diameter that is polynomial in relation to the group's size. Systematically put, if a group G has at least one abelian subgroup of size at least √(|G|), then the majority of finite groups in the specified size range will have a diameter that is polynomial in relation to the group's size, specifically with a specific constant of proportionality. It is worth noting that abelian subgroups of large size are quite common, especially in nilpotent groups, which serve as a key component of our proof for the majority of finite groups having a logarithmic diameter. Additionally, we provide an independent proof that for any given positive integer k, the majority of finite groups of size at least k will have a largest abelian subgroup of maximum size less than or equal to √(k), specifically with a specific constant of proportionality. A related but distinct concept known as the linear rank of a group is also introduced and compared to the diameter of the group. A notable exception to this similarity is seen with groups that have an abelian subgroup of maximum rank, which can result in a linear rank that exceeds log_2(|G|) and thus also results in a diameter that is polynomial in relation to the group's size. This study presents a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor leverages a ring voltage regulator to accurately measure thermal resistance at room temperature, enabling the calculation of any given temperature based on junction temperature measurements. The design employs a 1-bit SAR ADC and a 4-bit DAC to determine the (Vth0, Ith0) pair of a test MOSFET, allowing for the calculation of (Vth0, Rth0) and subsequently any given temperature. The proposed temperature sensor leverages a 65nm CMOS process to achieve a temperature range of 0 to 120 degrees Celsius, with a measurement period of approximately 10 minutes. The design includes two variants: one with an external resistor for user-defined (Vth0, Rth0), and another with an (Vth0, Rth0) array to enhance scalability and reduce user-defined development time. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed temperature sensor in a real-world application, showcasing a measurement accuracy of ±1.5 degrees Celsius in a commercial SoC. Furthermore, the design exhibits a measurement period of approximately 10 minutes, with a ring regulator measurement period of 5 minutes and a ADC conversion period of 5 minutes. The proposed temperature sensor occupies an area of 0.062mm^2, with a supply voltage of 1V and a supply current of 9.5microA. The benefits of using this temperature sensor in a system that employs adaptive voltage and frequency scaling are also highlighted, showing that a 10 degree Celsius reduction in junction temperature can lead to a 20x increase in system lifetime. The design and implementation of the temperature sensor, as well as the experimental results, are thoroughly discussed in the subsequent sections. A temperature sensor based on this design has been manufactured and is available for testing purposes. Interested parties can contact the authors for further details. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, as certain cores exhibit higher masses when compared to their parental cloud averages. We propose a model where protostellar cores have more significant masses than starless cores, with a possible mass threshold of approximately 7 times the solar mass. This mass disparity might result from the longer timescales required to halt the mass growth of cores once they surpass this threshold, allowing for the transition from star formation formation. Furthermore, we observe a positive correlation between core masses and the surrounding environment's density, which could be an indicator of the mass distribution necessary for cores to interact with nearby molecular flows and initiate outflows. The Dragon infrared dark cloud offers valuable insights into the early stages of low-mass star formation, particularly the pivotal 10,000-year period during which stars, cores, and gas evolve in tandem. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the recurrences in positive definiteness can be determined by examining the changes in the space dimension, in comparison to previous methods that required separate verification for each space dimension. The underlying principle is linked to the properties of Jacobi polynomials, considering their ability to produce derivatives and integrals of the same polynomial, thus ensuring the consistency of positive definiteness. This breakthrough has far-reaching implications for the application of space-filled methods in machine learning, particularly in the context of spherical spaces. The underlying idea of recurrences in positive definiteness can be applied to a broad category of systems of special functions, including but not limited to the Gegenbauer polynomials on spherical spaces, also including the scenario where the underlying space is Euclidean or hyperbolic. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to capture target word dependencies by introducing a new attention sub-system that pre-computes and stores reference distributions for target words. These stored distributions can be readily used to model word sequences and avoid the difficulty of long sequential dependencies. Moreover, the model automatically adapts to different data sets and can be combined with existing look-ahead techniques, such as recursive recurrent neural networks and waiting words. Experimental evaluations on NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks demonstrate significant improvements in translation accuracy. In particular, the proposed model achieves a 3.3% absolute increase in the Chinese-to-English translation task, outperforming the LSTM baseline by 10%, and also attains the current state-of-the-art performance on the English-to-German translation task, exceeding the previous best result by 5%. System code is available at https://github.com/zhukaisheng/LookAhead-NMT.

Recent observations of the rare decay J/ψ → γν$\bar{\nu}$ suggest that light sterile neutrinos might be present, adding a layer of complexity to the standard J/ψ two-body decays. We investigate how this phenomenon could affect the B→J/ψX decay distribution by incorporating J/ψ decays into invisible particles, considering four possible scenarios for the sterile neutrino mass and mixing strength. Calculations take into account J/ψ decays into all possible two-body channels, accounting for both hadronic and radiative modes, with the exception of J/ψ → γe+e-. By comparing theoretical predictions with available B decay data, we establish lower bounds on the sterile neutrino mass and mixing parameter: for a single sterile neutrino, the minimum required mass is approximately 20 MeV, with a corresponding upper limit on the mixing parameter of 4.5 × 10^-4, while for multiple sterile neutrinos the minimum mass is around 60 MeV and the mixing parameter is less than 2.9 × 10^-4. Although these limits are already fulfilled by other constraints, our study demonstrates that future J/ψ production rates from rare B decays could serve as a significant source of rare neutrino interactions. Our research also highlights the potential for discovering light sterile neutrinos at the B-factory, providing valuable insights for future experimental investigations. The growing complexity of time series analysis is caused by the increasing frequency of multivariate functional time series, whose different components vary over time and exhibit distinct patterns. The need for a more advanced technique that can handle these diverse patterns has led to the development of multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA), a robust method that has been successfully applied in various fields, including economics, climate science, and medicine. Despite its benefits, MFSSA has primarily been used for non-parametric analysis and lacks a theoretical foundation to support its purposes and effectiveness. This study fills this gap by establishing the asymptotic properties of MFSSA under general conditions, including its convergence and consistency in both $\mathbf{l}^2$ and sup-norms. Additionally, we demonstrate that the MFSSA can be employed as a data-driven method to select the number of components and estimate multivariate functional autoregressive models. We support our findings with numerical examples and empirical results from a real-world dataset. Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align with data graph topologies, offering a simplified framework. Two types of convolutional layers are examined – standard GCNN and Graph Attention Network (GAT) – and their equivalent matched filter forms are derived. This equivalent form provides valuable insights, revealing the sources of GCNN overfitting and GAT overfitting/under-smoothing – along with possible remedial solutions. Our concise and clear framework can be easily extended to other GCNN variants, offering a foundational view of these networks. Elastography is an advanced imaging technique used to analyze tissue elasticity by analyzing sound wave reflections from tissues compressed and relaxed. The technique has seen significant advancements in recent years and has become a valuable tool in medical diagnostics. High-resolution elasticity imaging can be achieved using phased array ultrasound systems through the Synthetic Aperture (SA) technique. However, SA faces significant challenges in areas with high tissue movement and close-to-sensors tissues. A new method called Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture (VSSA) has been proposed to enhance elasticity imaging by modifying SA. This approach simulates the use of linear array ultrasound systems by creating virtual sources using phased array systems. As a result, VSSA can improve resolution, reduce grating lobes, and increase flexibility in data acquisition. Furthermore, VSSA can be applied to elasticity imaging by controlling compression and release movements of tissues. The technique has been tested on phantom tissues with the phased array system and the linear array system VSSA. The resulting elasticity images from VSSA showed a significant improvement in resolution, a decrease in noise, and increased accuracy when compared to traditional methods. The technique has also been validated by comparing its data with that obtained from the linear array system on real human tissues. The tissues used were breast, liver, and prostate tissues. The elasticity images obtained from VSSA showed a high correlation with those obtained from the linear array system on all three types of tissues. The technique has the potential to revolutionize elasticity imaging by making it possible to use phased array systems with limited apertures. This could lead to the development of portable and cost-effective ultrasound systems for elasticity imaging. The technique also presents opportunities for improving other medical imaging modalities that use ultrasound systems with phased arrays. The VSSA technique can be applied to different types of elasticity imaging algorithms, including phase elasticity imaging, real-time elasticity imaging, and magnetic resonance elastography. The technique has been tested on different types of tissues and ultrasound systems, including phased array systems with and without linearizing circuits, and phased array systems with and without tiring coils. The technique has been validated on different types of tissues, including phantom tissues, breast tissues, liver tissues, and prostate tissues. The technique has the potential to be used in different medical applications, including breast elasticity imaging, liver elasticity imaging, prostate elasticity imaging, and brain elasticity imaging. The technique has been tested on different types of ultrasound systems, including phased array systems with linear arrays, phased array systems without linear arrays, and phased array systems with linearizing circuits, and phased array systems

Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as two distinct yet related paradigms for accomplishing the same computational tasks. This interconnection suggests that there might be a compelling basis for considering them as equivalent expressions of the same underlying evidence for computation. This concept is referred to as equivalent evidence for computation or "equivalent evidence" for short. Equivalent evidence provides a fresh perspective on the relationship between algorithms and proofs. It offers a novel framework consisting of a set of fundamental rules that generate both imperative algorithms and the steps in natural deduction proofs. It is also a natural foundation for developing various forms of formal systems including algorithms, logic systems, and verification methods. This paper serves as an introduction to the theory of equivalent evidence. It begins with the analysis of the interconnection between algorithms and proofs. This is followed by an in-depth exploration of equivalent evidence. Some examples of applicable theory are also provided, including the generation of algorithms from natural deduction systems, the derivation of soundness and completeness proofs, and the development of a verified compiler. All relevant material is illustrated through the application of equivalent evidence to the task of creating a verified compiler. All the concepts discussed are put into practice through the compilation of a given programming language into a formal system that can be used for proving the correctness of the code, with the compiled code then being interpreted as both the evidence for the correctness of the code and the algorithm for its compilation. All the theory discussed is put into practice through the development of a verified compiler called the Dependence Logic Compiler, or DepLoC for short. DepLoC is capable of compiling a substantial subset of first-order dependent type theory into the Miniml programming language. It also generates the proof of correctness for the code it compiles, with this proof being based on a formal system that is guaranteed to be sound and complete due to the underlying nature of the theory it is based on. The development of DepLoC is carried out using the theory of equivalent evidence. It is hoped that the introduction of equivalent evidence will contribute to the ongoing discussion about the relationship between algorithms and proofs. It is also hoped that DepLoC will serve as a proof of concept for the practical applications of this theory. It is worth noting that the name "logic" in the name DepLoC refers to the type of logic on which it is based rather than its general purpose. The algorithm employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ bits to track cluster centers and yields an approximate solution to the problem, with the space requirement dependent upon the closeness to optimal of the desired solution. When the algorithm is terminated, it provides a set of $k$ updated center points representing the clusters. We further establish that the performance of our algorithm is comparable to an ideal solution obtained through the help of an 'ideal' streaming algorithm that has access to unlimited storage capacity. We derive the space complexity of this ideal algorithm in relation to several constraints, including the size of the dataset, storage capacity, and the number of clusters, utilizing which we determine the required storage to achieve a specific level of accuracy in the solution. Specifically, we demonstrate that in the presence of the streaming constraint, a space complexity of $O(\log N)$ is unavoidable for achieving an error of $1/\poly(N)$ from an optimal solution when processing datasets of size $N$. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. With this hierarchical model, the number of considerations in the aggregated game is drastically reduced, enabling the development of remarkably effective and lightweight algorithms. Specifically, we derive a linear program to solve the individual state-level games and an linear system to solve the aggregated level games. This leads to a range of advantages, including a significant decrease in computational time and memory requirements. We also gain substantial insights into the game's dynamics and probabilities. Ultimately, this novel approach yields exceptionally brief and efficient algorithms, resulting in a marked improvement in the computation time needed to reach a Nash equilibrium compared to existing methods. Experimental evaluations in vast grid worlds demonstrate the substantial benefits of this innovative approach. Systematic methods for validating the macro-states and avoiding computational overload are also presented as well as a method to handle dynamic grid worlds. The overall framework is highly versatile and can be applied to a wide range of related problems, including optimal flow in grid networks and the maximum flow problem in graph theory. We believe this novel framework offers a pioneering step in addressing large-scale stochastic games and presents a range of exciting research opportunities. Due to the inevitable impact of forward and sometimes excessive radiation in electromagnetic interactions, lepton colliders with high-energy capabilities beyond a few TeV may face significant issues. As a result, there has been a growing interest in exploring the behavior of QED at very high energies within a finite angular acceptance, particularly in relation to advanced lepton colliders. In this paper, we discuss the fundamental limitations of QED in the deep relativistic regime, focusing on the effects of forward radiation on observable physical phenomena. We also examine the consequences of gauge radiation on physical quantities such as the cross-section of Compton scattering, the pair production of fermions, and the scattering of vector bosons, all within a finite angular acceptance. We demonstrate the finite lifetime of particles and the finite lifetime of the $\mathcal{e}^+\mathcal{e}^-$ pair in this context. We also explore the potential for a lepton collider to operate in a regime where the center-of-mass energy can exceed the pair production threshold for a particular lepton flavor by utilizing large beam currents and implementing suitable acceptance cuts, and we outline various strategies for achieving this. We also examine the prospects of such a collider for discovering evidence of the $\mathcal{e}\gamma\rightarrow\mathcal{W}\mathcal{W}$ process, which could indicate the presence of a new physics sector that could become visible at future lepton colliders with very high energies. We propose the term "luminosity lifetime" to describe the measure of the strength of a lepton collider, representing the duration for which a collider can maintain a certain level of luminosity at very high energies, and we examine the factors that influence this property, including beam current, acceptance cuts, and the resulting pair production of fermions. We believe that understanding the limitations of QED in the deep relativistic regime, particularly in relation to forward and excessive radiation, is crucial for the successful operation and optimization of future high-energy lepton colliders. We also anticipate that the concept of luminosity lifetime will become an essential performance metric for these colliders. We have made our numerical data available online as part of this research. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Our research demonstrates the potential risks and rewards of
multi-task learning in the context of dynamics models within the framework of
RBMDT, while also providing a foundation for exploring this topic in the future. System codes are available at https://github.com/zhongyuyu1998/rbmdt. Our results can be used as a baseline for future research aimed at improving the performance of model-based multi-task reinforcement learning settings. Our study and codes aim to contribute to the ongoing discussion on the applicability and limitations of shared dynamics models in multi-task scenarios. We then move on to examine how these theorems have been used to demonstrate the limitations of attempts to formalize certain aspects of mathematics, specifically the impossibility of fully formalizing truth within a formal system. We also explore some historical context surrounding these results and their development, as well as the notable contributions of mathematicians like Hilbert, who sought to provide a consistent and complete foundation for mathematics, and the impact of these theorems on their efforts. Finally, we discuss some of the formal arguments underlying these theorems, starting with a derivation of the Diagonal Lemma from a single natural axiom, as well as a derivation of the first incompleteness theorem from the Diagonal Lemma. We then move on to prove the theorems related to Godel's first incompleteness theorem, including Rosser's strengthened form and the strengthened form due to Kleene and Rosser. We also examine the relationship between Godel's first incompleteness theorem and the theorems on the limitations of formal systems in regards to truth and provability. We conclude by examining some of the criticisms and potential issues with the original formulations of these theorems, as well as some of the resulting extensions and generalizations, including those made by mathematicians such as Shoenfield, Osherson, and Boolos/Burton. We also explore some of the historical and philosophical context surrounding these results and their implications for our understanding of mathematics, as well as the development of intuitionistic and other non-classical formal systems. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to automatically generate artificial counterparts of inverse problems using the MRI scan of a rat, and applied it to a challenging problem involving a deep neural network. Our main contribution presents a way to sample from the posterior distribution by using a non-linear generative model, specifically a deep convolutional generative adversarial network, which allows for a direct and efficient training due to its simple and adversarial training framework. The efficiency of this model allows for a seamless integration with existing solving methods that work on the real-world domain, resulting in a fast and accurate inversion of the forward problem. The proposed technique is demonstrated through applications to MRI reconstruction, deep compressed net reconstruction and natural image reconstruction. The code is available at https://github.com/tingseon/DeepPosteriorSampling. The performance of the algorithm is assessed through both quantitative and qualitative metrics, and the source code is provided to ensure the reproducibility of the results. The future directions involve exploring the integration with other solving methods and enhancing the model to accommodate various prior knowledge. The algorithm's versatility can be observed through its versatility in modeling diverse data domains by simply exchanging the training sets. The interstellar medium is home to scattering screens taking the shape of 
large, thin clouds that can be identified by measuring the time it takes 
for a signal to be reflected and a signal to be received. Researchers used 
pulsar scintillation patterns to locate and study these screens in the 
interstellar medium surrounding the VELA-PULSAR. Data from 15 years of 
observations revealed that screens are divided into two categories based 
on their size and thickness: a large screen measures about 10 to 20 solar 
masses in both mass and radius, and is composed of a dense cloud that is 
completely engulfed by a much larger cloud that measures about 10 to 20 
parsecs in both mass and radius. Additionally, screens are found to be 
oriented vertically and move at a pace that is one tenth the speed of a 
star moving in our galaxy, and are found to be stable for approximately 
10 to 20 million years before they break down. Furthermore, by calculating 
the amount of matter that makes up the interstellar medium surrounding the 
VELA-PULSAR, researchers found that screens account for about one percent of 
that total. Lastly, by examining the composition of the screens and the 
interstellar medium surrounding the VELA-PULSAR, researchers found that 
screens are more dense than the average interstellar medium in our galaxy. 
This knowledge about the interstellar medium surrounding the VELA-PULSAR 
could be applied to the study of other pulsars that exhibit strong 
scintillation patterns. This knowledge about the interstellar medium 
surrounding the VELA-PULSAR also provides valuable insights into how the 
interstellar medium in our galaxy evolves over time. This research was 
conducted by examining data from a radio telescope in West Virginia that 
observed a pulsar named VELA-PULSAR for 15 years. This research was

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNNs, ensuring the model's periodic signal components are consistent with the input frequencies. Secondly, a hybrid approach is used to extend the frequency range beyond the training data, enabling the model to effectively handle zero-padding segments. Experimental results demonstrate that QPNet exhibits improved pitch control and generalization capabilities compared to standard WN and other generative models, enabling the generation of high-quality waveforms for a wide range of inputs. The model's effectiveness is showcased through applications in text-to-speech synthesis and music synthesis. The code for QPNet is available at https://github.com/zhengzhongrusen/qpnet.

Deep neural networks excel at recognizing visual elements, including the absence of certain features, which poses a challenge when attempting to train models that rely on hidden or distant objects, such as sound sources in videos without audible sounds. To overcome this challenge, a learning technique called positive weighting was recently introduced, enabling the model to focus on hidden objects by design. However, the current implementation only considers the situation where the model fails to detect a hidden object and does not effectively utilize the technique for object exclusion. To address this limitation, a new positive weighting variant is proposed, referred to as hard sample mining, which incorporates the technique into the standard supervised learning framework. By assigning higher importance to difficult, accurately labeled data, the model becomes more adept at locating sound sources, as demonstrated by improved performance on the sound source localization dataset, particularly when objects are partially hidden or distant. The proposed method demonstrates substantial performance gains, with an average precision increase of 24.5% in difficult object exclusion scenarios. The model also exhibits a high AP of 0.64 in sound source localization, surpassing human performance for the first time. The code is available at https://github.com/zhengzhong114/positive-weighting. Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been largely based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations lack rigorous mathematical foundations, and previous research revealed that standard graph convolution operations are actually equivalent to those in Euclidean spaces, albeit with different parameter settings. This paper provides a rigorous derivation of hyperbolic graph convolution and GCNs based on the geometry of Borel, and further explores their connections to Euclidean equivalents. Moreover, a novel and more efficient hyperbolic graph convolution is proposed, and experimental results show that it outperforms existing methods for multiple datasets. We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
social context. Similarly, we demonstrate that our delay discounting model
reduces to a special case of the Weibull distribution delay discounting model,
with its parameters linked to the average and shape parameter of impulsivity. 
Both of these findings open up possibilities for examining the underlying
dynamics of our new model using existing analytical methods. We also introduce a
new metric for assessing the elastically of delay discounting, which we use to
analyze the variations in our model. Furthermore, we discuss the differences
between our model and existing delay discounting models, before moving on to
present simulated and real data showcasing the elacticity of our model. 
Finally, we outline potential future research directions related to our model,
including applications in neuroscience, economics, and game theory. Systematic
reviews on delay discounting and impulsivity, as well as our supplementary
materials, are available at https://osf.io/p39fc/. We hope this work will 
stimulate a comprehensive meta-analysis of the delay discounting literature.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature. Furthermore, we outline the relationship between temperature and energy, highlighting how a negative temperature can arise when the system's energy exceeds a particular threshold, compared to a two-level system with constant coupling. We also examine the special case where the system's energy is evenly distributed, demonstrating how temperature becomes independent of the system's parameters. Finally, we discuss some common misconceptions surrounding negative temperature and provide an overview of its related statistical properties. Both mathematics and physical intuition are used to explore these properties and concepts, making this report accessible to a broad audience interested in statistical mechanics and thermodynamics. Schematics and graphs are included to visualize key concepts and facilitate a deeper comprehension of negative absolute temperature. Despite its abstract nature, this report remains grounded in fundamental theory, offering a hands-on introduction to this intriguing topic of negative temperature.
